speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER OF JAPAN AND PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by leave of the house I should like to mention the presence in the gallery of various distinguished visitors including Hon. Hayato Ikeda, the Prime Minister of Japan, and his charming wife. The Prime Minister is accompanied by the foreign minister, Hon. Mr. Kosaka. This is the first visit the Prime Minister has made to Canada, and because of his very busy schedule his visit will be brief. It is my hope that a further opportunity, not too long removed, will again bring him to our country to enable him to know Canada and the Canadian people better.
The Prime Minister of Japan, together with the foreign minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I have had useful talks this morning with respect to matters of common interest and concern. Canada's relations with Japan have been, as the house knows, particularly close in recent years. We have a similarity in approach to international problems; we have close and ever increasing mutual relations in trade. Indeed, during the past four years the increase in trade between our countries has amounted to 40 per cent. Last year the total trade between Canada and Japan was almost $290 million, and I believe it will continue to expand to the mutual benefit of both our countries.
Within the past two or three years there has been an increasing number of Canadian visitors to Japan and Japanese visitors to Canada. The result has been an improvement in the understanding that each country has of the other. Another, but not the least, of the links between our countries is the fact that some 26,000 Canadian citizens who are making valued contributions to Canadian society, industry, the arts and professions are of Japanese origin, deriving much of their cultural heritage from Japan, Canada's nearest neighbour across the Pacific.
I believe, and that belief is intensified on each occasion I meet with leaders of the various countries, that these meetings are
most valuable. Particularly is that so at this time. Close co-operation is necessary among the leaders of the countries which believe in democracy because, if Mr. Khrushchev is to be believed, we are now entering into the potentially momentous remaining six months of this year which will be of great importance to the nations everywhere in the world, and in particular to those who believe in the maintenance of democracy and parliamentary government and those abiding principles to which Japan now gives its adherence.
I wish, therefore, to express a very wholehearted welcome to the Prime Minister. I can say this: having talked with him yesterday and today, I believe Japan has a leader wise and far seeing, who is dedicated to the principles of democracy.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER OF JAPAN AND PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side in the opposition share wholeheartedly and most warmly the welcome that has been so fittingly expressed by the Prime Minister to the Prime Minister of Japan, his wife, the foreign minister and all the members of his party. I am sure all Canadians also want to share in that welcome.
One of the happiest developments, I think, since world war II has been the growth in political and economic relations between our two countries. We all hope there may be even a strengthening in these political relations and an expansion in these economic relations. Japan and Canada are two Pacific countries now in more than a geographic sense. We stand together in the Pacific, in the United Nations and indeed in the world for freedom, democracy and peace.

maintopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER OF JAPAN AND PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this group joins with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in extending a hearty welcome to the Prime Minister of Japan and his colleagues, and through him sends greetings to the people of his country.
As a member of the Canadian delegation to the interparliamentary union meeting held in Tokyo last fall I, with the other members of the delegation, will long remember with great satisfaction our visit to a beautiful and hospitable country. Our association with the Japanese people left us all filled with admiration for their progressive ideas, their industry, their charm and their unmatched

Bank of Canada
hospitality. I think I can best express the feelings of the Canadian delegation by saying this:
When Time, who steals our years away, Shall steal our pleasures, too,
Fond memories of those days will stay And half our joys renew.
On behalf of this group, Mr. Speaker, I express the hope that the visit to Canada of the Prime Minister of Japan and his colleagues will strengthen the ties between our nations and will result in agreement on economic and other matters that will further cement and strengthen our present bonds of understanding and friendship.

subsubtopic: REPORTED CLAIM TO SHEIKDOM OF KUWAIT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in view of the implications involved, whether he has anything to say about the announcement made by Prime Minister Kassem of Iraq regarding the taking over by Iraq of the newly independent sheikdom of Kuwait.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORTED CLAIM TO SHEIKDOM OF KUWAIT
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. As members of the house are aware, the United Kingdom government announced on June 19 that it had signed an agreement with the ruler of Kuwait cancelling the Anglo-Kuwait agreement of 1899 which recent developments had rendered obsolete and inappropriate. The exchange of notes between the United Kingdom and Kuwait by which this was effected, however, stated that relations between the two countries would continue to be governed by a spirit of close friendship, and reaffirmed the readiness of the United Kingdom government to assist Kuwait if the government of Kuwait should so request.
We have not yet received any official reports on the statement reportedly made in Baghdad yesterday by Prime Minister Kassem in which he laid claim to Kuwait as an integral part of Iraq. If, indeed, a dispute does exist between Iraq and Kuwait, I should naturally hope that the parties concerned would refrain from any action which would exacerbate the situation, and that the recognized international procedures would be followed for a peaceful settlement.
It so happens that our ambassador to Lebanon, Mr. Beaulieu, is now in Baghdad in the course of presenting his credentials as the newly appointed ambassador to Iraq.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: MRS. MALONEY-STATEMENT ON REPORTED DANGER OF DEPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a question was asked on Saturday by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. The answer is as follows.
On April 14, 1961 Mrs. Frances Maloney, a citizen of the United Kingdom and colonies was ordered to be deported on the expiration of her prison sentence. Although there is no provision for an appeal against a deportation order such as the one issued to Mrs. Maloney, I ordered this case to be reviewed by the general board of immigration appeals. As a result of this review and because of information provided in the written representations of Mr. W. A. McLennan, M.P., I decided to suspend the order of deportation for a period

of six months to give this woman an opportunity to rehabilitate herself.
Mrs. Maloney was released from detention on Friday, June 23.

speechtext: CREATION of vacancy in office of governor

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-114, respecting the Bank of Canada.

He said: Mr. Speaker, when I spoke on this matter in the house on June 14 I opened my remarks with this observation:
I should prefer to speak on an occasion of this kind with restraint. I do not wish to add to the injury which X believe, and believe with deep regret, the governor of the Bank of Canada has done to himself. Least of all would I wish to see any prolongation of controversy, particularly political controversy, in relation to the Bank of Canada.
It is in that spirit, Mr. Speaker, that I speak today in moving second reading of this bill. First let me make it very clear that there has at no time been a personal aspect to the present issue. There has been an attempt in the press and elsewhere to dramatize this issue and picture it as a Coyne versus Fleming issue. It has been no such thing at any time. There is no personal element whatever in this issue, and there never has been.
I say that notwithstanding the fact that in the attacks which the governor has been making upon the government in recent days he has singled out the Minister of Finance for special mention. Let me make it very clear, Mr. Speaker, that throughout this entire situation I have acted as the spokesman of the government, on the instructions of the government, carrying out decisions of the government, decisions that were not lightly arrived at.
On the other side let me make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that the bank as such has not been involved save to the extent to which the governor has, I say improperly, embroiled it in a controversy that has assumed a political character. On the contrary, the board of governors of the bank has taken a clear line and the governor has acted in a manner diametrically opposed to the views expressed by the board of directors of the bank in a resolution passed on June 13.
Therefore this bill is not, as it has been represented in some quarters, the outcome of what is called a feud. There has been no feud. So far as I personally am concerned I have endeavoured to work with the governor of the bank in matters in which our respective positions required contact. Certainly this is not, as it has been represented in at least one journal, the outcome of "a long struggle for economic power between two men". Mr. Speaker, statements of that kind are simply nonsensical. So far as differences exist, and of course there are deep seated differences, there was no acrimony in these differences until the governor injected it in his attacks commencing on June 13.
The real issue presented to parliament, Mr. Speaker, is one not simply of government versus governor. It is that in the broad sense. It is more specifically an issue of government plus board of directors versus the governor.
Governor of Bank of Canada In a more complete sense it is the government serving the public interest, plus the board of directors serving the best interests of the Bank of Canada, versus the governor in his determination to cling to office, unwanted, for six months more.
I say, Mr. Speaker, and I speak with deep regret here, that after being afforded every opportunity to go quietly, decently and with dignity, the governor has chosen to force an issue before the public and into parliament. He has defied the government; he has defied the board of directors in the most deliberately provocative manner. In this situation either the governor must go, and go now, or the government must go.
They should have gone long ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Parliament must decide who governs this country.
Here, Mr. Speaker, let me refer to an observation appearing at page 2201 of the Hansard of the present session, an observation for which I am indebted to the Leader of the Opposition. He said:
If the governor cannot agree with the general policy which the government desires him to implement, then the governor has no alternative, of course, but to resign.
Note the words:
-the governor has no alternative, of course, but to resign.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I did refer to that quotation when speaking in the house on June 14. I find there has been some liberty taken by the Hansard printers with the quotation and it reads, not that "the governor has no alternative, of course, but to resign", but that "the government has no alternative, of course, but to resign".
How right they were.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition might consider this an improvement, but it is not what he said on the occasion when I quoted him, at page 2201 of Hansard.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister is quite correct and I should have made that correction at the time. It is a regrettable inaccuracy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was not a matter for correction by the Leader of the Opposition. This was my quotation of his speech on this occasion, so I do not hold him responsible. The governor of the Bank of Canada is not required to account to the sovereign electors of Canada for his administration, but the government is. We will not accept responsibility for the governor and his actions when we have lost all confidence in him. The government has no power, under the law of this

Governor of Bank of Canada parliament, to remove the governor. That power is reserved to parliament, and to parliament alone. Parliament, sir, must now decide.
In presenting this bill to the house it has therefore been deliberately drawn in a form which will present the issue to parliament for determination in its clearest and most direct form. The measure is stripped of nonessentials and presents the house with the opportunity and the challenge to make a clear cut decision. The one clause in this bill reads:
The office of governor of the Bank of Canada shall be deemed to have become vacant immediately upon the coming into force of this act.
Mr. Speaker, it will be observed that effort has been made to deal with this issue in the measure as impersonally as possible. The governor is not mentioned by name. As I said, this measure presents the issue in a clear and direct form. Other questions can be resolved in due course and at the proper time. All other questions depend on the outcome of this issue before parliament. The issue presented by this measure is essential; the decision on it must precede anything else.
In the statement which I made on June 14 I laid certain facts before the house in relation to the matter. I shall enlarge somewhat today, though clearly and briefly, I hope, on the facts as they pertain to the issue now before the house.
When the present government came to office on June 21, 1957, the present governor of the Bank of Canada had already been in office for two and a half years. He had been associated with the tight money policy which we who now sit on the treasury benches had, when we were in opposition prior to 1957, attacked in parliament. Nevertheless, having come to office, we resolved to work with the governor as far as it was possible to do so. I have no wish to speak personally of the present governor. No one will ever say that he is an easy man to work with, but the government has done its best to work with him. He is a man of very great ability, but I think many people have found him sadly lacking in judgment and in ability to see the other person's point of view.
In the winter of 1957-58 I conveyed to him a request for an easing of the requirements respecting the liquidity reserves of chartered banks. That request, which was designed by the government to ease tight money, was rejected by the governor firmly and angrily. That sent me scurrying to the Bank of Canada Act-particularly in the light of things I had been arguing in this house while in opposition about the relationship of the Bank of Canada and the government in matters pertaining to monetary policy

and money supply-only to find that parliament had there given the government no power over the bank in such circumstances. Hon. members will understand the effect of this situation in the light of subsequent events which I may take occasion to mention.
In his annual report for the year 1957, which reached me on the last day of February, 1958, or the first day of March, in the middle of an election campaign, the governor chose to insert a couple of paragraphs in which he firmly asserted that there had never been a tight money policy. I had to make the decision as to whether that report should be released to the public in the middle of an election campaign. The government was widely dispersed. It was customary to release the annual reports of the governor of the Bank of Canada in the month of March. I knew very well that if that report was released in the middle of an election campaign, assertions of that kind on a subject which was a burning issue in the 1958 election as well as in the 1957 election would be seized upon by the Leader of the Opposition and an endeavour made to make political capital out of them.
I had to make that decision, and I reached the decision to allow the release of that report in March, 1958, in the middle of the election campaign. I did not intend to have anyone tell me afterwards that I had endeavoured in any way to suppress views which had been put forward by the governor of the Bank of Canada. That report was released. It was broadcast and, of course, the anticipated result immediately followed. The report had not been public more than a matter of several hours before the Leader of the Opposition in that election campaign seized upon this political manna from heaven and sought to make political capital out of it.
I am sure there are those who will say, with the benefit of what we know since, that the government in those circumstances ought to have asked for the resignation of the governor at that time. The fact is that we as a government could not compel his resignation. Only parliament could do so. In the light of what has happened since, perhaps we ought to have taken steps at that time. Perhaps there were other occasions when we should have done so. I am sure that had we known our efforts to carry on and make the best of the situation would be frustrated, as they have been, and that this matter would eventually come before parliament for the kind of decision the house is being asked to make today, we should all have agreed it would have been better if this issue had been brought before parliament earlier.

We did hope for better relations and we desired, above all, to avoid creating controversy involving the Bank of Canada. We attached, as a government, the highest importance to the bank and its functions. It was a creation of a Conservative government. We recalled that under the previous governor and under the same statute there had been harmony and co-operation between the governor on the one hand and the government on the other, between the bank on the one hand and the public on the other. Therefore we resolved to carry on and hope for the best, knowing that the governor's term of office would in any event expire on December 31, 1961. Let me tell the house that as far as my responsibility is concerned I have done my best to carry on in a co-operative attitude.
In the field of debt management, the field for which the government holds responsibility, the governor of the bank has rendered to the government good service. In this field the bank operates as an adviser to the government and as its agent. It supplies technical assistance. The government takes full responsibility in this field. Often when advice was tendered we did not accept the recommendations so far as they related to interest rates or prices. Nevertheless I wish to make it very clear that the government takes full responsibility for what has been done in the field of debt management, and we have in respect of this field of operations made full use of the bank's very efficient facilities.
In the second place, in the field of foreign exchange operations, here again the Bank of Canada acts as the government's agent; and in this field, which is directed by Mr. Ras-minsky, the deputy governor of the bank, the bank has operated very efficiently. The government, of course, takes full responsibility for what is done in this field.
Third, in the field of fiscal policy which is, of course, the government's responsibility, the bank, through the deputy governors, has been consulted on general aspects of budget policy in the writing of the budgets. It has never been the practice of the governor him-helf to sit in on these discussions. In this field I stress again that the responsibility is entirely that of the government.
Fourth, in the field of monetary policy, let me be very explicit. The government's relations with the governor of the Bank of Canada in regard to monetary policy and monetary operations have been set within the framework of the position which the governor took in that meeting to which I referred in the winter of 1957-58. The Bank of Canada has operated monetary policy, in full control of it. The government has had no control
Governor of Bank of Canada over monetary policy. The bank authorities were always willing to explain and defend their operations, but the policy followed was always the policy of the governor. The government had not determined it. Dealing with various criticisms which have been made during discussions in the house, I have endeavoured at all times to make it clear that the government was not to be associated with monetary policy for the reasons I have mentioned.
Until the autumn of 1959 the governor had not made a practice of making public speeches, but at that time be began to do so. For the next year and a half he made them with increasing force, frequency and fervour. Never was I or any other member of the government consulted at any time in any respect whatever in regard to the making of those speeches or their contents. They quickly attracted public attention, which increased with each of those public utterances, principally because they were devoted almost entirely to fiscal, not monetary, policy and thus entered upon one of the most controversial subjects in the whole political spectrum. The governor did not directly attack the government, but it was not long before the government was bearing the full weight of his criticisms and strictures. He contended time and again with ever increasing vehemence that the country was suffering from wrong fiscal policies and the absence of needed fiscal programs. Such, under our constitutional system, Mr. Speaker, are the responsibility of the government, not the responsibility of the Bank of Canada.
The press and the public quickly grasped the significance of the governor's criticisms. Indeed, everybody in Canada seems to have been well aware that the effect of those speeches was to direct criticism at the government; everybody seems to have been aware of this except the governor himself. The opposition in this house seized on the governor's statements and debated them in this house with a view to exploiting the embarrassment, the political embarrassment, which the governor was causing to the government. You have an example, Mr. Speaker, in the debate in this house on February 20 and 21 of this session. You have another example on March 22, in a discussion on the annual report of the governor. These statements of the governor were variously pictured by the opposition as government policy, which they were not, or as showing that the governor was at odds with the government; or they were made the occasion of taunting the government.
Perhaps, in the light of what has now happened, Mr. Speaker, the government should have intervened drastically earlier. However, we were very reluctant to attempt to place a curb on the governor, knowing well that in

Governor of Bank of Canada the political atmosphere which was becoming more tense on the subject we might have been ourselves denounced by the governor or the opposition, or both, for attempting to muzzle free speech when it was critical of government policy.
It has to be remembered that the governor is not a civil servant but the official head of a most important public institution, so we endeavoured patiently to live with this situation hoping that the governor might adopt a wiser course, and one more in keeping with the responsibilities of his high office, or that December 31, 1961 might come soon. In the meantime the governor was being warned by members of the board of directors of the bank that the course he was pursuing was involving him and the bank in politics; as one director put it to the governor, involving the governor "right up to his neck in politics".
The governor did not yield to advice from this quarter to discontinue those speeches. I was receiving communications from investors in the United States, in the United Kingdom and Canada who were very disturbed by the governor's pronouncements against foreign investment in Canada. It was as difficult to explain to them that the governor spoke for himself alone and not for the government as it was for them to understand this fact. For example, in January of this year I made a speech in New York to the Canadian club of that city, designed to clarify Canada's attitude toward foreign investment and to reassure those investors in the United States who had investments in Canada, or who contemplated useful investments in Canada, as to this country's intentions and attitudes. In March the governor made a speech in New York which was interpreted to the very opposite effect from my speech in January.
I am sure I do not need to remind the house that the fiscal policies which the governor was advocating in his numerous public utterances were in their nature isolationist, bureaucratic, anti-American, centralizing. They could have done violence to our international obligations; they would have provoked retaliation against Canada by other countries; they would have increased taxes, restricted trade, increased the role of government in business in this country, and would have centralized more authority in the federal government at the expense of the powers and authorities of the provinces under our constitution.
The suspicion inevitably grew that he was building up some kind of case. His speeches seemed to fall more and more into a pattern openly challenging the government. The memorandum which he sent to me on February 16, and which he made public on June 19, bore in tone, content and timing all the 

earmarks of an indictment and challenge directed against the government. The appearance of creating self-serving evidence was very strong. I deliberately refrained from public comment on the governor's public utterances, accepting much unjustified criticism in consequence, and I did so for the sake of avoiding controversy affecting the Bank of Canada.
This, however, did not deter the governor from pursuing with undiminished vigour the same course which had given rise to controversy. It reached the point where I was frequently asked by serious people whether the governor was deliberately seeking to undermine the government. I was placed in the equivocal position of appearing to defend the governor because of my desire to preserve the bank from the weakening effects of harmful political controversy, while at the same time I disapproved strongly of the public course the governor was following.
That position could not continue. It was obvious that parliament and the Canadian public would be entitled at some time to expect from me an accounting for the position of the government in a situation in which the governor appeared to be openly challenging the government.
It was, even in the face of the views that many serious people expressed to me, hard for me to believe that a man in such circumstances would deliberately attack the government or seek to undermine it. Personally, for myself, at that time I expressed the view that the governor was not doing this for the deliberate purpose of seeking to undermine the government, but I did hold him responsible for the creation of this result, whether or not it was by deliberate design on his part. And in the circumstances, Mr. Speaker,-and for this I have no apology to make to anyone-I could no longer give the governor my confidence.
We met at my request on Saturday afternoon, March 18. He gave me his categorical assurance that all communications between us, including the memorandum he had already sent me and my reply dated February 20, were confidential. I shall say only that our discussion was frank and I spoke plainly.
His published letter to me of June 9 that he had stopped making public speeches then is to be qualified, if it is to be regarded as a virtue, by his accompanying statement that he had no further speeches scheduled at that time. However, he did say as he has said in the letter of June 9 that he has now published:
I saw nothing Improper in the making of speeches or in anything that I had said.
So, Mr. Speaker, the governor on his part, while expressing regret that his speeches

might have hurt the government politically, asserted that he withdrew none of the things he had said in his speeches.
It became increasingly clear to the government that the governor had so deeply involved himself and the Bank of Canada in political controversy that there could be no possible redemption of the situation as long as he remained governor. The government was engaged in formulating a budgetary program of far-reaching proportions about which I wish to say two things. First, that program could not be fully implemented without strong co-operation on the part of the Bank of Canada. Second, that program was built upon certain fundamental principles which were widely at variance with the views repeatedly expressed by the governor and held by him firmly, yes, even dogmatically, in his numerous public utterances.
If we credited the governor with sincerity in these views that he expressed, and I told him that I did, it was abundantly clear, therefore, that if he was sincere he could not be expected by the government to support a program which the government deemed necessary in the public interest. The government had long since decided that it could not approve his reappointment as governor on the expiry of his term on December 31. It now concluded that there was no other course open to it in the national interest but to ask for the governor's resignation.
In this situation the government made inquiry concerning the pension provision made for the governor. It was then for the first time that the government or myself became aware of an amendment to the pension bylaw passed by the board of directors of the bank at its meeting on February 15, 1960. At my request I was furnished with an extract of the minutes of that meeting and, as I explained to the house on June 14, as found at pages 6315 and 6316 of Hansard, the government was shocked to learn that as a result of that bylaw the governor purported to become entitled immediately on the conclusion of his service to a pension for life on retirement of $25,000 per annum, compared with a pension entitlement prior to that meeting under the same circumstances of just under $12,000 per annum. The fact that the governor, though not participating in the board proceedings at which the bylaw was passed, and notwithstanding the fact that he possesses veto powers under the Bank of Canada Act, did not inform the government of its passing nor publish the bylaw or notice of it in the Canada Gazette was in the view of the government a serious dereliction of duty on his part.
On May 30, in pursuance of a decision taken by the government, I invited the governor to
Governor of Bank of Canada my office where, in the presence of the deputy minister of finance, I informed him with deep personal regret-and I emphasize that, Mr. Speaker-that the government, after full consideration of the matter, had decided to ask for his resignation. I further said that I was prepared to give him the reasons for the government's decision if he wished those reasons.
The governor in his public statement of June 13 has given the impression that the only reason related to his pension. He has had something to say on this subject of which I should remind hon. members. Referring to me, he said:
To aid me in my consideration of this matter he-
That is myself.
-said the cabinet were upset by the fact that the bank's board of directors had taken action in February, 1960, to improve the conditions of the pension which, according to the rules of the bank's pension fund, had always been provided immediately on the termination of service of a governor or deputy governor. He said the government were considering what action to take in the matter of the pension, had not yet come to a decision, and wanted my resignation before they came to a decision.
That last statement is not correct. I certainly did ask for his resignation. I did say that we had not come to a decision, but I did not say that the date of the resignation related to the decision. He continued:
Mr. Fleming also said the cabinet were of the view that I had failed to discharge the responsibilities of my office in allowing the board of directors to take the action they did take unanimously and after thorough consideration in amending the pension fund rules, an action which the Department of Justice had said was entirely within the powers of the board. This slander upon my integrity I cannot ignore or accept.
That passage is the only one in the public statement issued by the governor on June 13 in which he purports to give the reasons which I stated on that occasion had led the government to ask for his resignation.
No, it is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is on this interpretation that certain articles have appeared in the press and statements have been made over the radio. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, and I do hope I can make this clear for all to understand, that in the course of our discussion on May 30, one hour in length, I gave the governor five reasons. In the order in which I advanced them they were as follows: First, in his speeches he had shown that he was openly at odds with the government on important policy questions. Second, he had embroiled the Bank of Canada in political controversy. Third, his views were incompatible with far-reaching programs upon which the government was about to embark. Fourth, he did not possess the confidence of Canadian financial institutions with which the Bank of

Governor of Bank of Canada Canada must work. Fifth, his pension arrangements, and failure to notify the government or the public of the bylaw increasing his own pension.
These were the five reasons. Each of these was discussed as fully as the governor wished on this occasion. I stress that the government had given the subject very full consideration, and that he was asked to submit his resignation in time for the board of directors to take action on it and to appoint his successor at its meeting scheduled to be held in Quebec city on June 12 and 13. I stressed the fact that in the view of the government it would be most undesirable that there should be anything like an interregnum at a time when the co-operation of the bank was required in the fulfilment of these important and far-reaching programs.
Would the minister permit a question at this point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am trying to finish by one o'clock. There will be an opportunity for questions when we go into committee on the bill.
My question has to do with-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The governor asked me three questions which with my answers I related to the house in my speech on June 14, which will be found at page 6353 of Hansard, for that date. He said he withdrew nothing of what he had said in his speeches. After an hour of quiet discussion, the governor asked for time to think the matter over. He said nothing about any attack on his character or his integrity. We shook hands and quietly said goodbye.
In his statement of June 13 he denounced my reference to his failure to report his pension increase as a slander upon his integrity which he could not ignore or accept. People who hear words that they regard as slander upon their integrity usually react very swiftly to them. There was no such reaction on the part of the governor in our hour-long discussion on this occasion. Our conversation was carried on quietly throughout, and we shook hands and parted with, on my part, an expression of personal regret that matters had given rise to this situation.
I received no direct answer from the governor, apart from several letters of an obviously self-serving nature, carefully timed to reach me on the morning of June 12, and which he has since evidently released to the public. I think his letter of June 13 was mentioned in this house by the Leader of the


Opposition, that letter having reached the Leader of the Opposition apparently as soon as it reached me.
In taking the action that he did on June 13 the governor rejected firmly and flatly the resolution passed by the board of directors of the Bank of Canada by a vote of 9 to 1 requesting his resignation.
It was dictation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a false statement, Mr. Speaker. It was no dictation. The board of directors of the Bank of Canada had reached a decision, as responsible men would under the circumstances. What we have just heard from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is the same kind of insult to the intelligence of these responsible men on the board of directors of the Bank of Canada as the governor himself directed toward those persons.
The governor issued his public statement on June 13 at a time when the board had, at his request, suspended its discussions on the resolution and before it had adopted that resolution to request his resignation. He deliberately timed the release of his statement, according to his own admission, so that it would hit the House of Commons at its opening that day, and would reach the public before the Minister of Finance could make any statement on the question.
What is the minister quoting from there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am quoting from a statement that was made by the governor on this occasion.
I had taken elaborate and careful precautions to avoid publicity in order to spare the governor embarrassment to the utmost possible extent. Had the government wished to make a scapegoat of him, as is falsely alleged by some malevolent and prejudiced persons, the government would certainly not have followed this considerate course. It was by the governor's deliberate act and intent that this question became a public issue. He has pursued his objective and attracted to it the maximum publicity regardless of the harm it may do to relations between the Bank of Canada and the government and between the Bank of Canada and the public. He has sought to keep himself in the headlines, and has evidently enjoyed the personal publicity which he has attracted to himself. He has repeatedly made himself heard by the entire nation not merely in his own defence but in audacious attacks on the government. No public servant in Canada's history has ever been heard so much and so often. There have been many hearings, including an appearance just two months ago before a Senate committee.
But not before the banking and commerce committee of the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I guess the hon. member for Essex East is glad now that he did not appear before that committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The appearance was denied by this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Since June 13 the house has debated this subject. It was debated on June 14. Having openly declared war on the government in his statement on the morning of June 13 and in his press conference that night in the board room of the Bank of Canada, the governor has pressed his political campaign against the government with ardour. Had he resigned he would have regained his full right to debate the political issues publicly. He did not wait, however.
Making full use of the facilities of the Bank of Canada and continuing to draw his salary as governor, he used his office in the bank as a base for operations against the government. He has made very wide distribution in Canada of his statement of June 13, mimeographed by the bank, presumably at bank expense, mailed out in Bank of Canada envelopes stamped by the postage meter of the Bank of Canada. Some of these envelopes have been sent to me by recipients who have expressed indignation and disapproval of this improper use of bank property. It would be interesting to know what the cost to the bank has been in mounting this political attack against the government. Let me say that if the facilities of the bank had been used on this scale and in this way, not to attack the government but to aid it, I am very sure that the opposition in this house would have been up in arms because of this abuse. That is not so now.
In the publicizing and distribution of June 19 of this memorandum he sent me on February 16 in confidence, a confidence which he reaffirmed on March 18, I say that the governor acted most improperly. I say that the governor's conduct since June 12 has of itself been such, without regard to what had happened before that time, as to have made necessary his dismissal from his high office.
Mr. Speaker, I see that it is now one o'clock and I have been unable quite to finish.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last point with which I was dealing prior to 90205-6-445
Governor of Bank of Canada the luncheon recess concerned the events transpiring on and after June 13; and in the light of the actions taken by the governor in this period I had submitted to the house that the governor's conduct since June 12, of itself, has been such as to have made necessary his dismissal from his office.
I turn now to certain specific points. This morning I made mention of this subject of the slander upon his own integrity that the governor purports to find in the reference to his failure to notify the government of the action taken by the board of directors on February 15, 1960, in increasing his pension by more than double. I leave it to the house, Mr. Speaker, to decide whether or not this is to be regarded as a slander. Certainly no such expression was used at any time before the governor resorted to this expression on June 13.
I disclaim completely the kind of article that has been written in certain quarters picturing what has been done in this situation as a "political assassination". That, I regret to say, is the title that appeared in The Economist of London on June 16 over an article written by the Ottawa correspondent of that journal, namely Mr. Michael Barkway. I wish to make it very plain that there has been no such thing as character assassination here. The governor did not on May 30 interpret to that effect anything that was said on that occasion. Never a word or hint did he drop of interpreting anything that had been said as being a slander upon him or upon his integrity. If there has been a slander in his misinterpretation of it, then the broadcasting of it is his own personal responsibility.
The next point I wish to draw attention to is the fact that on this very subject, in his statement on June 13, the governor chose to go completely outside the scope of the issue that he saw between himself and the government in relation to his tenure of office as governor of the bank. Having used the sentence to which I have referred concerning the alleged slander, he added:
It appears to be another element in a general campaign of injury and defamation directed against crown corporations, their chief executive officers and other public servants. I cannot and will not resign quietly under such circumstances.
I ask the house to draw its own inference from the fact that the governor, who was saying at this time that he should have been permitted to continue in office until the end of December, chose to go completely outside the scope of the Bank of Canada or its relations with the government in order to engage in a political accusation against the government concerning its relations with other national institutions or crown corporations or persons heading them. I leave it to the house

Governor of Bank of Canada to decide whether, under those circumstances, it was proper for the governor to engage in that kind of deliberate, omnibus, general political accusation against the government. This accusation came at a time when he was asserting that the government should have had confidence in him and in his co-operation. It is an interesting sidelight on that kind of assertion on his part.
The next point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, is that the government takes full responsibility in the realm of fiscal policy. Its program-I refer to the kind of program that was introduced in this house last Tuesday evening-requires effective co-operation of the authorities in the fiscal and monetary fields. The governor's campaign has been aimed at absolving monetary policy of responsibility for economic conditions and for action to meet economic conditions. He has deliberately sought to throw on to fiscal policy the full burden of meeting economic problems. In my respectful submission, this is not only an unsound and untenable proposition but it was part of the campaign to pillory the government. He has carried it on in his statement of June 15. He states:
As I see it, the trouble has not been in the field of monetary policy-
And so on. Further down he states:
What has been lacking so far is adequate action in the field of fiscal policy.
If that is not a deliberate attack on the government, I do not know what can be an attack. What is required, in the view of the government-and it was implicit in what I said to the governor at our meeting on May 30-is that for the solution of Canada's present economic problems there must be a co-operative approach by the authorities in the fiscal and monetary fields.
As to the extent of the deep seated differences of approach to economic problems and responsibilities of the authorities in these two respective fields, fiscal and monetary, I shall not repeat what I said last Tuesday night. It is on record on pages 6666 to 6668 of Hansard, and any further comment on this subject no doubt could be more appropriately reserved for the budget debate. In that, Mr. Speaker, I include any comments upon the February memorandum which the governor released a few days ago.
Next, Mr. Speaker, I have drawn attention to the governor's disclaimer of the responsibility of monetary policy for meeting economic conditions. But the governor in his statement of June 15 chose to go further, and indeed he has sought, as I have indicated, to throw responsibility off his shoulders and all responsibility on to the government in a field where the view of the government is 
that responsibility must be shared and action must be co-operative. Well, sir, he may say now that he disagrees with the view I have expressed in this house, that the government has not had responsibility for monetary policy. He has in these statements undertaken to express disagreement with my interpretation in that respect. All I have to say, Mr. Speaker, is that he was well aware of that interpretation. It was given to the house under the circumstances of the situation at the time in various debates in this house over the past two sessions, and although he must have been well aware that statements were being made in Hansard, never once did he express himself to me personally as not sharing the view I was expressing, or taking issue with it. This statement that he has recently made in this respect is the first intimation that has ever come from him to me of a view that the responsibility for monetary policy was a responsibility of the government and not simply that of the Bank of Canada under the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act.
Next, Mr. Speaker, let me draw attention to what the governor has said in his statement of June 19. Referring to the February memorandum which he released-the confidential memorandum-he has said:
1 have been anxious to have constructive discussion of these matters but the Minister of Finance has not found time to discuss the substance of them with me.
Mr. Speaker, I must take issue with that statement. A number of these matters that are referred to in the February memorandum were discussed last autumn at meetings in which the governor and others and myself participated. There were, I should say, a large number of various items that appeared in the February memorandum which had already been discussed. Let me say this, that having read the February memorandum I did not need extended discussion to satisfy me that such a program as he was putting forward in broad outline in that memorandum was in many of its aspects not acceptable to the government. I have referred to the fact that it would have involved a breach of our international obligations; that it would have provoked retaliation against Canada by other countries; that it would have restricted our trade; raised taxes; involved more governmental intrusion into business in this country, and would have necessitated for its fulfilment a federal intrusion into the affairs of the provinces, and other reasons.
It was not necessary for us to have extended discussion in the light of those facts. But let me draw attention to this; that when the governor complains that I was not sitting down and talking to him at length on the contents of that memorandum, I asked him-

this is when we met on March 18-if he had made any attempt to call me, telephone me, or make any appointment for the purpose, and the answer of course was in the negative. He had chosen, rather, to sit in his office and write these letters, and then complain that he was not being properly used because I had not sat down to discuss these questions with him at length.
The next passage in the statement of June 19 I think is of interest to the house as well.
It proceeds:
He-
That is referring to myself:
-has also for four years refused to allow the banking and commerce committee of the House of Commons to study my annual report or to examine my views as to whatever extent might be desired by members of parliament.
Mr. Speaker, that statement is untrue.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was in 1959 that a question was asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. He did not press it. He asked if the government was going to refer the report to the banking and commerce committee. A halfhearted question was asked in the 1960 session by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. It was only in the present session that this matter has become an issue.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is entirely wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the governor of the Bank of Canada makes this assertion that for four years I refused to allow the banking and commerce committee to study the annual report, what he is saying is not true.
At which time did you not refuse?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me refer to something one of my predecessors had to say on this subject. I am putting this on the record to refute the statement of the governor and also to clarify issues that have been beclouded in this house in the present session. There has been only one year when the annual report of the governor of the Bank of Canada has been referred to the banking and commerce committee for study. That was in the year 1956. Let me draw attention to the year 1957, not after the change of government but the session of 1957 that preceded the general election and change of government of that year. The request was made at that time for reference of the report to the banking and commerce committee. I refer to Hansard of February 14, 1957 at page 1277. The hon. member for Greenwood put this question to the then minister of finance: 90205-6-44SJ
Governor of Bank of Canada
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. In view of the fact that I understand the Bank of Canada report for 1956 will be down shortly, will the minister be able to tell us that the banking and commerce committee will have an opportunity of having the report presented and discussed by the governor of the bank, as was done last year?
The answer was:

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall give consideration to what appears to be a request.
Then we find that the matter was revived a month later. Hansard of March 11, 1957 indicates at page 2064 that the hon. member for Greenwood returned to his question and asked the minister of finance:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of Finance whether it is the intention to have the governor of the Bank of Canada, now that the report is out, appear before the banking and commerce committee as he has done in the past?
To this question the minister of finance, Mr. Harris, made the following reply:
Mr. Speaker, I think I may have slightly misled the house-
He was obviously referring to what he had said earlier on February 14, which I have read:
Mr. Speaker, I think I may have slightly misled the house and the hon. member for Greenwood by a reference I made in answer to a question such as this earlier in the session. I find that it has not been a custom for the governor of the Bank of Canada to appear before the banking and commerce committee. It is true that the former governor and the present one have appeared before it on occasion but a good deal less frequently than I had thought when I made the answer. It would therefore not be correct to say that it has been customary, although on occasion it has been done. I shall consider whether or not it ought to be done in this case.
That is the end of the quotation and having considered it he did not propose that the report go to the committee.
Dissolution came.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Dissolution did not come for another month. I think that puts that matter in its proper light.
To what I have already said in reference to debates in this house, let me add this further comment on what the governor has said. Never once in all these years did the governor say anything to me about wishing to appear before the banking and commerce committee or wishing his annual report to be referred to the banking and commerce committee or to any other committee. This statement of June 19 is evidently calculated to give the impression that he was telling me he wanted to appear before the banking and commerce committee to discuss his annual report and that I did not let him.
Such impression could not be further from the truth; and when the governor talks about

Governor of Bank of Canada my refusing to allow the banking and commerce committee to study his report, if he is referring to anything that passed between us in this regard I have to say categorically that nothing of this sort has passed between us. If he is referring to debates which took place in the house, then I have to say to him that this is an intrusion into political debates in the house that ill becomes a man who aims to cling to office as governor of the Bank of Canada.
What is more, his statement does not accord with the facts, as the records of this house will plainly show.
The only time the governor ever talked to me about appearing before any committee ol the House of Commons was not in relation to his annual report or to the banking and commerce committee at all; it was in relation to his appearance before the industrial relations committee of the house on June 9, 1959, when he was called as a witness in relation to the investment policy of the investment committee under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I may say that on that occasion he expressed himself to me in terms of outrage-that is not too strong a word-over the shockingly unfair way in which, he asserted, he had been treated in that committee that morning by the hon. member for Essex East who, the governor said, had made lengthy speeches instead of asking questions, and who would not give him an opportunity to answer the questions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister what he is quoting from?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The comment of the governor himself arising out of that experience.
Did you write it down at the time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wrote it on the tablets of my memory and it is very plainly written there.
Your memory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, that is the fact.
I would like to have the opportunity of questioning the Minister of Finance in the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would love to have the opportunity of exposing the hon. member for Essex East and all the shillyshallying he has done on this subject for a long time.

Let us go to the
committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the attitude which the governor took in relation to the kind of questioning which was directed to him by the hon. member for Essex East on June 9, 1959.
According to your say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The next point
which perhaps merits mention was the observation in the governor's statement of June 13 that he has always co-operated with the government and would, of course, do so. This is a case where the governor invites the government to believe that he has never failed to co-operate. Although he has carried on this campaign which has embroiled the Bank of Canada in controversy and has put himself plainly at odds with the government on basic questions of policy, he is asking the government to believe that his co-operation can be counted on at a time when he is accusing the government of having slandered him and of having carried on a general campaign of injury and defamation against crown corporations. In the face of that, and all it amounts to, he asks that he be permitted to continue in office and that his protestations of readiness to co-operate should be accepted at face value. This assertion that he had always cooperated and was prepared to co-operate was never made until some days after a request had been made for his resignation.
I have found, to my great regret, that the governor has not possessed the confidence of the public and of those institutions in the Canadian economy with which the Bank of Canada must work. I shall not go into the question of the attacks which have been made upon monetary policy in this country by those in the academic field who are students and authorities of this subject, but I would point to the fact that there is a reflection of the relationship of this issue to public finance in what has happened in the bond market since this matter became public by the act of the governor on June 13. The bond market has been stronger since that time. Bond values have been rising and interest rates have dropped slightly.
It must be plain to all concerned that there is a dispute, and a deep seated dispute, between the governor and the government here. I refer to the statement made in this house by the Leader of the Opposition on February 20, as reported on page 2201 of Hansard:
If the governor cannot agree with the general policy which the government desires him to implement, then the governor has no alternative, of course, but to resign.
There may be one question remaining. Suppose a case arises where the government on its part says there is a deep seated dispute between itself and the governor with respect

to general policy. Suppose the governor then says oh, well, I really should not be interpreted as having attacked government policy or as differing with it; I am ready to cooperate; I say there is really no deep seated difference between us. In these circumstances who is to judge whether there exists in fact a dispute, a deep seated difference in policy? Again I am indebted to the Leader of the Opposition for supplying the answer to this question. He did so at a television conference, broadcast from Ottawa last Thursday evening. From the script I quote the two following questions and answers, the answers being supplied by the Leader of the Opposition.
Who is to be the judge of whether there is or is not a dispute? If the government says, yes. there is a dispute, and the governor of the Bank of Canada says he knows of none, whose judgment-
A. Oh, the government's views must prevail in these matters. The government, of course.
Another question:
Q. You take the position, then, that if the government asserts that there is a dispute the governor of the Bank of Canada must resign?
A. I think that if there is a dispute of that kind the governor of the Bank of Canada should resign, of course.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Read on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me make it very clear that the government asserts that there is a dispute with the governor of the Bank of Canada.
After four years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are deep seated differences to which I have now made reference, and in the face of this situation the house should be under no misapprehension. We say there is a dispute and, therefore, having regard to the principle put forward by the Leader of the Opposition himself, it is the duty of the governor to resign. Indeed, that is the only course.
Perhaps it would have sufficed if instead of my detaining the house at such length I had simply read the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition on February 20, told the house that in the view of the government there is a deep seated dispute between us, and then referred to the further statement of the Leader of the Opposition that the government is the judge of whether there is a dispute, and that if the government says there is a dispute the governor must resign. That would have been a complete presentation of the case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister having quoted part of my answer, I wonder whether I might ask him-
Governor of Bank of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am making my speech. The Leader of the Opposition will have an opportunity to make his, and we shall be in committee later on and there will be opportunity there for questions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On a question of privilege-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say that this regime must, in the public interest-Mr. Speaker, there is no question of privilege whatsoever.
You are the Speaker as well as the executioner. Sit down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition rises on a question of privilege. I have to hear him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege because the minister has quoted from a statement I made the other night. He has quoted only one part of the statement and has drawn his conclusions from that part. I am now asking him to complete the quotation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is a matter of explanation which the Leader of the Opposition will have an opportunity to present himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition knows perfectly well that I read in full two questions and his answers to those questions, and any attempt to pretend otherwise just does not agree with the facts. The Leader of the Opposition may repent now of the answers he gave, but his answers are there and they were recorded at the time. They are very plain and categorical on the point.
You don't dare to read the next paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
You don't dare to read it; you don't dare to.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Hon. members cannot prescribe the way in which another member presents his speech, provided it is in accordance with the facts.
A deliberate attempt to mislead the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has been acting this way lately, Mr. Speaker; he has been going into hysterics almost every day in the house. It is evident that it is time to administer some kind of sedation to him. He is quite unable to control himself.
I say in conclusion that in the public interest the present regime in the Bank of Canada must give way to one in which the good relations which previously existed between the bank and the government and between

Governor of Bank of Canada the bank and the public will be restored and co-operation in fiscal and monetary policies will prevail.
Sir, the present governor of the bank was appointed to his high office by order in council. That order in council is P.C. 1954/ 1789. It is dated November 18, 1954, and it purported to appoint the present governor as governor at a salary of $50,000 per annum, the appointment to take effect as from January 1, 1955. Under section 6, subsection 2, paragraph 3 of the act, his appointment is for a term of seven years during good behaviour. In an office so exalted the standard of good behaviour, Mr. Speaker, I think you will agree, should be of the very highest. It is known to all that the governor has lost the confidence of the board of directors of the bank; he has lost the confidence of the government, and he does not possess the confidence of a good many sections of the public with which the Bank of Canada is expected to work.
Enough has been said, I believe, Mr. Speaker, to demonstrate that the governor has not fulfilled the terms of his appointment in November, 1954; that the public interest is suffering from his continuance in office; that the government itself has no power to remove him from office; and that in the face of his open defiance of requests from the government and from the board of directors of the bank for his resignation, only parliament can remove him. By the present bill parliament is asked to take that action, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question before he sits down? I should like to ask him just one question arising out of his statement. In view of the statements he has made, which have been contradicted by others, including the governor and directors of the bank, and in view of the desirability of clearing up these contradictions without delay, will the minister give the house the assurance now that immediately on the second reading of this bill it will be referred to the committee on banking and commerce where evidence can be taken and witnesses heard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will notice that the Leader of the Opposition has chosen to couch statements within the framework of what purported to be a question. I take issue at once with the statements he has made, which are not statements of fact or truth at all. When he says that the statements I have made have been contradicted by the governor and by members of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada he is not telling the truth. The answer to his question is no.
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) .1
Shame.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very short bill, but that does not mean that it is not a very important one. Some of the most important legislation in democratic history has been very short, and some of the most important attacks on freedom and democracy have been in very short bills; therefore the significance of this bill is not to be determined by its length. It reads:
The office of governor of the Bank of Canada shall be deemed to have become vacant immediately upon the coming into force of this act.
I leave aside certain doubts about the constitutional validity of a bill of this kind. It does not, of course, amend the Bank of Canada Act. We have been told in the house that that would be required to bring about this result. Indeed, you might find a case for argument whether parliament, if it passes this bill declaring this position vacant, is the only body that can fill it. According to this possible argument it remains vacant until parliament takes action to fill it.
I leave aside these legal points-they may be brought up later-to speak for some time, because the minister spoke for some time, on the substance of the bill and what is involved in it. And I hope, Mr. Speaker, I may be permitted to speak without those chattering interruptions to my left.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member interrupted frequently.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister told us that he was going to speak with restraint. In the light of his remarks, especially at the end of his long statement, I leave the house to judge how much restraint he showed in his personal attack on the governor of the Bank of Canada, and indeed in quoting not from a record but from his own memory of a statement purported to have been made by the governor of the Bank of Canada a long time ago.
At this time I do not intend to deal with many of the points the minister raised, but they will be dealt with; because the minister may have considered that he spoke with restraint, but we consider he spoke in a manner which requires to be answered, and he will be answered point by point. But I cannot forbear to mention two points in the minister's statement, one of which relates directly to me. He quoted from my television interview the other night, and I stand by what I said in that broadcast. But, as is his custom, he did not continue the quotation. I said, of course, that if there is a dispute between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the government, the governor should resign. I said

that in the House of Commons at a time when the minister was defending the governor against that kind of action. Then the next question was:
Do you think he should resign now?
My answer was this:
I say his usefulness is over as governor.
Of course that is true, Mr. Speaker. His usefulness has been destroyed by the government. Then I went on:
But Mr. Coyne apparently is determined to defend himself against certain charges which he believes reflect on his integrity. And that is why surely Mr. Coyne should have his day in court, and by in court I don't mean issuing statements which he feels are necessary because he isn't permitted to appear before a committee-and he states in one of his statements that he hasn't been allowed to appear before the banking and commerce committee to discuss the Bank of Canada report for four years.
That was a lie at the time. That has been denied.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I hear an hon. member saying "That is a lie". I take it he will withdraw that observation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member spoke in haste and will be quick to make amends for something that has universally been held to be contrary to parliamentary practice.
I withdraw the first part. I said that had been denied.
A lot of things have been denied.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Wrong again, Mike.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It certainly sounded like "a lie" here. In any event, that is what I said, that the minister did not quote; that before this dispute is settled in favour of the government the man who has been attacked should be given a chance to appear before a committee and defend himself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Will the Leader of the Opposition permit a question?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will answer questions, like the minister did, at the end if my statement. There is something else the minister said which should be replied to immediately. The minister made a great play in building up his case for this dispute between the bank and the government which has extended now over four years, on the fact that in 1958 the governor of the bank refused to take the action which the government asked the bank to take with regard to tight money and lower interest rates. He had some strong things to say about the governor angrily refusing to take certain action. It is surprising that the minister, having made that statement,
Governor of Bank of Canada did not take this opportunity to tell us the evidence on which it is based; because on June 21 we asked him a question on this very point. The hon. member for Welland put the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Page?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Page 6812. The question reads as follows:
1.	Did the Minister of Finance ask the governor of the Bank of Canada to increase the money supply on any occasions since June 21. 1957?
2.	If so, on what occasions?
3.	Did the governor refuse to accede to any such request?
4.	If so, which ones?
What did the minister say on that occasion? Compare this with what he has tried to say this afternoon.
Mr. Speaker, the communications between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance have always been regarded as privileged.
Then the hon. member for Welland put this question:
1.	Did the Minister of Finance ask the governor of the Bank of Canada to take steps to reduce interest rates on any occasion since June 21, 1957?
2.	If so, on what occasions?
3.	Did the governor refuse to accede to any such requests?
4.	If so, which ones?
This was the answer of the Minister of Finance:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to this question is the same as that given to the previous one.
The minister, however, purported to give an answer this afternoon, and the answer he gave this afternoon is contradicted by his own statement at the time. On February 14, 1958, according to a Canadian Press story the minister had this to say, and I quote from this report which has never been denied:
Whatever may have been said for the tight money policy in 1955 and 1956, it is evident that it does not fit the needs of 1958.
Then he went on to say this:
Money is more plentiful, credit is somewhat easier and interest rates have been reduced to a remarkable extent in recent months.
Does that look as if the Bank of Canada was not co-operating with the Department of Finance in these matters?
He just said that for the electorate, of course, during an election campaign.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, that was an election speech, and as the Minister of National Revenue, whose absence from the house and especially the reason for it we all lament, said on one famous occasion, "Election promises really do not mean very much".
This short bill which we have before us, Mr. Speaker, is the result that was made necessary by the difficulty, if you like by the

Governor of Bank of Canada mess, that the government has got itself into through its mishandling of this matter, through its customary ineptness and procrastination, this time extending over four years, in dealing with a problem through its customary procedure, its customary practice of allowing a problem to deteriorate until it becomes a crisis and then taking sudden and panic action to deal with it. This situation in which the government finds itself, this controversy between the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada, has already-the minister himself has said this- done harm to Canada's prestige and Canada's position, and I agree-
Good.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: -with the minister and with all members of this house, I hope, that this matter should be cleaned up with a minimum of delay. But it should be done in the right and proper way. Justice cannot be subordinated to speed, desirable as speed is in this case. I agree and I have just repeated that the governor's usefulness has ended as long as this government is in charge of finance.
Are you going to hire him back?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But the governor's usefulness has been destroyed by this controversy precipitated by the government, and I will go into that in some detail later. Because of that the governor has become a scapegoat, and he is becoming a scapegoat without an opportunity for an inquiry and without parliament being given an opportunity to inquire into all the facts, into the charges-and more have been made this afternoon-and the countercharges.
The bill makes no such provision before dismissal, provision for the right of inquiry, the right of every public servant to have an inquiry, whatever his position, before dismissal if he does not hold his position at pleasure, and the governor of the bank does not. Incidentally, the minister referred to the governor of the bank as a public official, which is correct. The Prime Minister referred to him incorrectly over the air the other night as a civil servant.
The governor of the Bank of Canada does not hold his position at pleasure. He holds it during good behaviour. When a man in his position is being forced out of office as he is by this legislation, then irrespective of the merits of the case he should be given an opportunity to state his case before a parliamentary committee because it is parliament, the high court of the land, which is being asked to take action. If parliament is being asked to take this kind of action, surely in simple justice the man concerned should be


given the opportunity to appear before a parliamentary committee. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I asked the minister once again after his statement this afternoon whether he would not ensure that the bill would be referred at once to a committee where evidence could be taken and witnesses could be heard. If he had said yes, and he should have said yes, that would have ended second reading as far as we are concerned.
Instead of hanging a man on the prejudiced statement of the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
