And, Mr. Speaker, this action, this denial of justice, this denial of the right to appear before a committee of the House of Commons which is asked to discharge this man, is being taken by a government which boasts so often about the bill of rights it asked this parliament to pass, one part of which includes words to the effect that no such act-Canadian act of parliament-order, rule, regulation or law shall be construed or applied so as to "deprive a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations".
Perhaps the Minister of Justice will tell us whether he has examined this bill in the light of the bill of rights and whether this bill, in the form in which it is presented to us and in the light of the refusal of the government to permit the hearing we have asked, is consistent with the letter or at least the spirit of the bill of rights.
The issue in this bill is not, as the minister tried to tell us this morning, who governs this country. There is no doubt about that. Parliament and the people govern this country. The issue is not who governs this country; the issue is how this country should be governed. The issue in this bill is not Mr. Coyne or his financial and monetary views. We on this side have criticized his views when the Minister of Finance defended him. The minister brought forward some evidence a few moments ago, and I am not quite sure whether he was in favour of Mr. Coyne or against him. He brought forward the statement which he said he remembered Mr. Coyne made, that it was outrageous the way we criticized Mr. Coyne in committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was the hon. member for Essex East in that committee to whom he referred.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister quoted the governor's statement which he remembered so well, which was not in writing, that the questioning of the hon. member for Essex East, who was speaking as a Liberal member of parliament, was outrageous.
It was.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Therefore the financial and monetary views of Mr. Coyne, we not having been given the opportunity to question them, have been sometimes criticized on this side of the house at a time when they were defended by the government, when the government refused to allow the governor of the bank to appear before a committee of the house for further questioning.
That is not the issue in the terms in which the minister put it before us. The issue is an historical issue of responsible government; of the control of the elected representatives of the people over the executive and the right of parliament to scrutinize every act of the executive, including any act which forces out the governor of the Bank of Canada.
By this bill the executive is seeking to make the elected representatives of the people rubber stamps, because they are being asked to take action without information, with the exception of that information which they receive from the minister who has put the bill forward. We are being told with respect to a matter of vital importance, the consequence of which may be with us for a long time, only what the Minister of Finance wishes us to hear, and on the minister's say so we are being asked to give a blank cheque to the government to control the bank without any parliamentary scrutiny. That is what we are being asked to do today, Mr. Speaker.
What excuse does the minister give us? On "The Nation's Business" broadcast the Prime Minister said:
Public servants are not the masters of the elected representatives of the people.
Mr. Speaker, that is perfectly true, of course. But here we have two chief public servants-the Prime Minister, who is a public servant, and the Minister of Finance, who is also a public servant-forgetting that they are public servants and telling the elected representatives of the people that we must declare the office of the governor of the Bank of Canada vacant and-this is the heart of the matter-without any reasons being given in this bill.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is no provision in this bill for scrutiny by a committee of the house. We are being asked to do this because one public servant, the Minister of Finance, has given us highly partisan and prejudiced accounts of his relations with the governor of the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
How ridiculous can the hon. gentleman be?
90205-6-446
Governor of Bank of Canada

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It certainly is ridiculous; there never has been such a ridiculous procedure put before this House of Commons.
Nor such arrogance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I agree with the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance in his effort to come to the defence of his minister.
The Bank of Canada is not a part of the executive; it is not under the control of the executive branch of government. Why is it not? The Bank of Canada is not a part of the executive because parliament decided that final control over the policies governing money supply should not be entrusted to the government in secret, but to parliament in the open. History demonstrates that control by the executive over money supply is one of the shortest roads to a dictatorship. That is why every free country has taken the most elaborate precautions to prevent the control of the supply of money falling into the hands of an arbitrary executive, free of any effective parliamentary scrutiny or control. What is the use of having parliamentary control of the right to tax if we are going to give the executive a blank cheque to start the printing presses rolling to pay their huge deficits?
Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada Act was carefully designed to prevent this from happening, and that is why it provided for a representative board of directors who were to be independent of the government. That is why the board and not the government was given the power to appoint the governor and deputy governor, which is something the minister carefully avoided referring to when he was talking about the appointments this afternoon, although approval of these appointments by the government is also required to ensure, it is hoped and has, indeed, been the case, the necessary harmony between the governor and the government. That is why the governor was appointed for a fixed term, subject to good behaviour, not subject to pleasure. Parliament intended the bank to be independent Of control in that sense and to act independently of government control within its own sphere, but not, of course, to act in a fashion that would frustrate the policies of a government. There is no difference between us on that score.
In other words there was to be harmony and co-operation between the government and the governor, because without that harmony and co-operation one can understand the difficulties that would ensue. If that harmony and co-operation could not be maintained, and if the governor did not resign voluntarily, a responsible government under our system has a clear duty to bring this

Governor of Bank of Canada situation at once to the attention of parliament, the source of all authority and control, and to propose suitable action which parliament could take, but only after due and proper parliamentary inquiry in accord with simple decency and justice.
The minister told us two weeks ago, and repeated with vigour this morning and this afternoon, that the necessary harmony has been lacking for four years between himself and the governor of the bank. However, until two weeks ago he kept that disharmony in secret from parliament, and denied every suggestion of the opposition that any lack of harmony existed. I will have something to say about that latter. There is plenty of evidence that can be produced in respect to the question of lack of harmony which so recently has been discovered and which now, four years after, the minister complains about very bitterly.
Information which came to us then for the first time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Essex East says, the information came to us for the first time in the last two weeks. This concealment by the minister from parliament is a self-confessed breach of the minister's duty to parliament. When this disharmony arose, as we are now told it arose years ago, surely then if the minister could not do anything about it the Prime Minister, the head of the government, should have stepped in and restored the position, if that was possible.
We do not even know whether the Minister of Finance told the Prime Minister about this disharmony over the years. We do know he is very sensitive himself about being told anything in respect to the administration of the bank and financing and all that sort of thing. We know from his words again this afternoon that although he had his assistant deputy minister at a meeting which dealt with pensions, when the minutes of the previous meeting were read, yet in spite of this kind of representation he himself did not know what was going on at that meeting of the board of directors. We do not even know what information the Prime Minister had about this fundamental disharmony. Surely if it exists-and it has existed for four years, we are told-the Prime Minister might have stepped in at any time, as any prime minister with a sense of responsibility would have done, and done his best to clear it up without the damage to the country and its prestige that has occurred by the events of the last two or three weeks. The trouble with this government is that it is too busy running a campaign to run a government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Where have you been lately?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the government were convinced that the governor of the bank was really obstructing government policies-and they claim to be convinced now; it is a kind of ex post facto conversion or conviction- parliament, as I have said, should have been fully informed, but it was not informed, and the governor of the Bank of Canada as head of an institution responsible to parliament, should have been given a full opportunity to explain his position and defend it. If he could not or would not explain his position and defend it satisfactorily, then and only then parliament should act. Instead of doing that-and that was the right course to follow-the Minister of Finance let the situation drift for nearly four years until his patience became exhausted or something else happened. He prevented the appearance of the governor before a committee of this house. Although he denied it this afternoon, the fact is that the governor of the bank did not appear before a commons committee during those four years. If there was this fundamental disharmony which we hear about now for the first time, why would it not have been the first desire of the minister to see that the governor of the Bank of Canada went to a committee of the house and explained his policies so that the government could explain to the committee where this disharmony lay and so that action could have been taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What action?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is unfair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the main issue in this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is very unfair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Are we going to suppress the right of inquiry, which is essential to the ultimate control of the Bank of Canada by the elected representatives of the people, or are we to hand that control over to be exercised in secret by a government with the record this government has had of lopping off the heads of able public servants?
If this bill is passed in this form, without any recourse to a parliamentary committee where witnesses can be heard and evidence can be taken, what will be the effect of this action on the prestige and morale of the public service? Let me repeat what I have already said. The governor holds his position during good behaviour, not at pleasure. In addition to the judges, there are only a very few public servants who are appointed during good behaviour. What does that phrase mean? It means that such public servants can be removed only for cause and not because they happen to displease the executive in the discharge of their duties.
What the minister is doing in demanding Mr. Coyne's resignation, or what he was doing on May 30 when he demanded Mr. Coyne's resignation, was the equivalent of calling in the chief electoral officer and saying this to him: "We are going to change the electoral law in a way we believe you will not approve, so please resign quietly and thereby maintain the dignity of the office and let us appoint someone who will do the government's will".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is exactly what happened in the case of the governor of the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ridiculous.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It was the equivalent of calling in the president of the C.B.C. and telling him this: "We have a new broadcasting policy that you will not like. It is too secret to reveal to you, it is true, but please get out quietly and make way for one of our friends". Mr. Speaker, the procedure followed in this bill is no better than that. It is true parliament has the opportunity to vote. Theoretically the bill could be defeated. But before the House of Commons is asked to vote we are being

Governor of Bank of Canada refused the right of inquiry into the nature of Mr. Coyne's alleged misbehaviour. We get that only from the minister himself, who will not I am sure complain when I call him, in this matter at least, not an impartial witness. This merely turns parliament into a rubber stamp for the executive.
If there are grounds for Mr. Coyne's removal, there is a proper way to do it. I have put it on the record and I repeat it because it is the heart of the matter. The proper way is that we have a full parliamentary inquiry at which Mr. Coyne as well as the minister, and members of the board, if you like, could fully and freely present their differences, if any, and be cross-examined. If that inquiry, which could be concluded very quickly-it need not take long-showed that there are legitimate causes for removal on the ground of misbehaviour, then parliament could and should take appropriate action to that end.
That action, I suggest, should not take the form of this kind of bill. That action, I suggest, would require two stages. First an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act, an amendment which we were told by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) not long ago would be required in this situation, to provide a procedure for removing the governor similar to that contained in the Judges Act, so we could not have this kind of situation in the future. Then a joint address of both houses with the full particulars which justify the removal of the governor.
That would be due process of law and it would help to preserve the necessary independence of the office of the governor of the bank and the assurance that the government was not tampering with the money supply for partisan or other improper purposes. It would also confirm, beyond the reach of contradiction, parliamentary control in such unhappy disputes. We have not that in this bill. What we have here is a return to the processes of despotism. This bill before us is in essence a bill of attainder, a procedure outlawed by the bill of rights in the United States constitution and not used in England since 1798.
This bill is introduced into this house by the governor's accuser, the Minister of Finance, and the accuser alone is allowed to give evidence before parliament. He alone passes judgment and to parliament is given the dignified and appealing role of executioner. This, Mr. Speaker, takes us right back to Tudor days.
It was not always thus in this house so far as hon. members opposite are concerned. Listen to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) in earlier days when he was in the opposition; listen to what he said on June 9, 1955, as reported at page 4563 of Hansard:

I ask the Prime Minister now: Do you have to circumvent the rule of law in order to achieve power under this legislation? Nothing of the kind! Have the powers, but in order to assure that no individual shall be discriminated against and denied equality before the law, to assure that the individual shall not be a puppet in the hands of the minister, give to the individual who is able to establish that he has been discriminated against a right of review by the courts of the land. Surely, we have not arrived-*
Said the present Prime Minister:
-at a state of mind in this country when parliament is asked to abdicate the rights of the courts for an indefinite time in the future in order to satisfy the desire for power of any minister or of any government.
Then again, in the same debate, as reported at page 4566 of Hansard, the Prime Minister had this to say:
With respect to constitutional power, read Burke. What did he say? What were his words? The tyranny of the majority is a multiple tyranny. No better answer can be given today than that. It is no excuse-
Said the present Prime Minister:
-that you have a big majority.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me look at some of the issues behind this procedure which we attack. This is the basic problem; it is basically the procedure which we attack. Let us look at some of the issues behind this legislation and what the minister said today justified the action he is asking the House of Commons to take. Let us look at the record. Apart from the procedure being followed, which is to be condemned, has the government made its case that the governor should resign? Has he in fact been non-cooperative in working with the government? Has he obstructed government policy? Is that the basic cause of the dispute?
If that is true-and the minister has stated it is true-it has been denied by the governor and it has not been proven at any inquiry. It has only been stated by the minister. The public evidence available to us-not that which we have secured from the minister alone-indicates that Mr. Coyne on May 30 and subsequently has been put up by the government both as a scapegoat and a target. After all, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing like publicly knocking down a bank president to take one's mind off massive unemployment.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is nothing like this kind of smokescreen and confusion to conceal the inefficiency of the government, its fumbling and bumbling in economic and other matters. The charge made and repeated this afternoon is that the governor of the bank was a proponent of restrictionist policies, tight money, high interest rates and all that.
That is what he said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Indeed the Minister of
Finance said specifically in the house on Tuesday last, I think it was, and again over the air the same night, that this was the main difference between him and the governor. I will quote his words again; he confirmed them this afternoon. He said:
Mr. Coyne's rigid attitude on the maintenance of high interest rates-
That caused all the trouble, and that is what he had to fight. "That is why we were incompatible", said the minister. I suggest that from the Minister of Finance this is hypocritical nonsense, and "nonsense" is one of his favourite words.
One of his virtues.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When the opposition in this house pointed out time and time again the dangers to the economy, at a time of recession, of tight money and high interest rates, the minister argued vehemently that our charge was false and absurd, that in fact interest rates were down, rather than up. If hon. members read Hansard for March 31, 1960, page 2671, they will find that was the minister's argument in this respect. In the debate on monetary policy last February to which the minister has already referred, the minister insisted that monetary policy and the question of money supply was a matter for the bank alone, not for the government. He threw aside all governmental responsibility.
The minister, therefore, could at that time have thrown the whole responsibility for any tight money, for restrictionist policies, onto the bank. He could in that debate have told parliament about the differences which he says now have existed for a long time. He could at that time have met head on the issue which he says now has existed for so long. Well, did he? If hon. members read the debate, they will find he did not do so. In direct contradiction to what he said in his budget speech of last Tuesday, he argued last February that bank policy had been such that the money supply as of December 31, 1960 was larger than it had ever been in Canada. He then praised the governor, he praised Mr. Coyne, and I note that as reported at page 2266 he added complacently:
V;ht"'c never has been the slightest interference by the government with bank monetary policy.
There never had been the slightest interference in the monetary policy of the bank. Presumably, this was because things were going all right. There was no reference to disagreement, no reference to fundamental disharmony. There never had been the
Governor of Bank of Canada slightest interference with monetary policy. Well, if that policy at that time and for years earlier had not been satisfactory, why did the government not intervene, at least to the extent of drawing its views to the attention of parliament? The government never interfere. Well, they are interfering now, though a few months ago the minister said that in the matter of interest rates the bank could not be criticized because the rates were not excessive compared with rates in countries such as the United Kingdom and the United States. Hon. members will find that statement reported at page 2207 of Hansard. Yet the minister said exactly the opposite when he made his budget speech last week. We are entitled to ask him: what kind of double talk is this?
Which time do you believe him?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We on this side expressed worry over the bank rate and over the monetary and fiscal policies of the government. We did the worrying and we did the criticizing and the Minister of Finance defended both the government and the governor. Indeed, he attacked me in February last, as will be seen at page 2688 of Hansard, for bringing the Bank of Canada into a centre of controversy by raising these question in the House of Commons, claiming I was unfairly attacking the bank and its governor which he was defending. This was in February, 1961; then on May 30, 1961 he asked the governor to resign. In view of this, could anything be more hypocritical than the minister's recent statements and his statement today about relations between the bank and the government? Could anything be more phony than this pretence of patient long suffering in the face of the governor's policy, which he was defending as recently as February?
What is behind all this? Well, the minister has suddenly become the champion of expansion. The governor, he says, is restrictionist. Perhaps that gives us a clue to the greatest conversion since the conversion loan of 1959. But the minister cannot get away from the record, and the record shows that it has been the opposition which has been pleading in this house for expansionist policies during the last four years and the government which has been opposing our expansionist proposals. Even with massive unemployment in a static economy, the minister was still possessed with the fear of expansionist proposals becoming a danger to the stability of the currency, leading to inflation. That was the burden of his sermons in those days. Inflation was the great villain,

Governor of Bank of Canada the great threat. And this was a view he shared at that time with the governor of the Bank of Canada.
On Tuesday last, however, at a time when expansion is in full flow according to the Prime Minister with a consequent increase of inflationary pressures, we no longer get a sermon from the minister on "work and save" or on the necessity of preventing inflation at all costs. We are to be spared these pedantic little homilies on financial responsibility. The text is now to be expansion. The minister has become complacent about the dangers of which he warned us earlier. There is not, he says, and I quote from his budget speech of the other night:
-any serious danger of inflation in present circumstances with so much unused capacity in our economy.
That is another conversion. He did not talk like this previously when there was even more unused capacity in our economy than there is today. Oh, no.
To conceal this about-face, to obscure the real issue, there had to be the smokescreen of a scapegoat. This was provided, without any consideration for decency or fair play, even to the extent of refusing to give the scapegoat the right to be heard and to defend himself against his accusers before a parliamentary committee. The elementary procedures guaranteed by the bill of rights were ignored, as were the procedures which give to the most junior civil servant the right to defend himself against charges before dismissal. The scapegoat was the head of a bank and bankers, of course, can be treated in this way without votes being lost. So goes the cynical reasoning.
So now we have what is called the Coyne affair to cover up this evidence of government misamanagement and ineptness and we are faced also with a refusal to allow any inquiry into this matter in a manner which would enable witnesses to be called and all the facts to be brought to light. This is all we are asking for on this side, but apparently it is not at all to the government's liking; that would not suit the government at all. The minister calls in the governor of the bank and says: get out at once; resign quietly, or else. This is the minister who a few months before had argued that he had nothing to do with monetary policy let alone the administration of the bank. Now he says: resign, or else.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There was no "or
else".
We can see the "or else". It is here.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The alternative was perfectly clear: resign quietly or we shall throw you out by act of parliament without there being a chance to appear before parliamentary committee. All we are asking is that this man and his accusers be invited by parliament, which is asked to take action, to appear before a committee of the commons where the facts can be ascertained.
Listen to what the minister said on February 21 on this point:
The government has no authority over the bank.
I particularly call the attention of the house to these observations by the minister which are to be found at pages 2256, 2257 and 2258 of Hansard:
The government must keep its hands off the bank just as it keeps its hands off the C.B.C.
That should have made us suspicious. Perhaps we were derelict in our duty by not attaching the proper significance to that observation by the minister.
Then the minister went on to say this as reported at page 2260. He asked himself the question:
Can the government change the management of the bank?
Then he answered it himself:
It cannot. The government has no power whatever, once appointments are made, to change them.
But it can bring the most extreme pressure on the governor to resign. Surely that is trying to change the management, and it is mere sophistry to argue otherwise. Therefore, the minister went to the governor without warning on May 30. He must have known it would provoke a crisis and he must have known, also, that there were only six months or so before the end of the governor's term of office. Knowing this, and knowing also that a committee of the board of directors of the bank was already working on finding a successor, the minister, in effect, says to the governor: resign at once, before the budget, which we have not discussed with you at all, but which we know you will not like even though we have not shown it to you. So resign at once.
The shabby insincerity of this attitude has been shown, particularly, by a question and answer in the house on February 21 as reported at page 2264 in the course of a discussion which is turning out to have been an important debate. The minister was speaking, and he was interrupted as occasionally happens by my friend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who said:
Does the minister agree with Mr. Ilsley's statement in 1941 that, in the event of a disagreement between the Bank of Canada and the government, it would be necessary for the governor to resign?

To which the minister replied:
No, no. Not in those terms-not at all.
Whereupon I intervened to say: "We do". That is, we Liberals. Then the minister made the following statement. I want to quote everything he said, not just a part; he quoted me in part but I shall quote him in full. He went on to say:
Unless, in the event of disagreement, the governor ... chose to resign.
Then he went on:
There is nothing that the government is in a position to do in that situation except to ask parliament to change the legislation, or wait for the expiry of his term.
This bill does not change the legislation; it does not alter the Bank of Canada, and the minister did not wait for the expiry of the governor's term.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is sophistry now.
A bill of attainder.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Let me turn to another matter. Need this crisis-and it is a crisis and a most unhappy one-ever have arisen? Of course the answer is certainly not, if it had been properly handled much earlier, and if there had been close and continuous contact between the governor and the minister. There was no such contact. The minister himself will not deny that. In the loss of such contact and in the face of this disharmony, as I have said previously in this debate, then it is for the Prime Minister to step in. If only the government had accepted its proper responsibility for monetary policy and exercised it at a time when, according to the minister now, Mr. Coyne was first proposing ideas and policies and making speeches of which the government did not approve. He was making speeches which included things we did not approve and we brought this up in the House of Commons. The minister, however, had nothing to say about the speeches in the house. But in 1961, I think it was in February or March, the minister did at last tell the governor to stop making speeches of this kind-
In March.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
-and the governor did. If the minister felt this way about the governor and his speeches and his policy, why did he wait until March, 1961? My own speech in this house on February 20, 1961 gave the Liberal view on both responsibility and policy. I emphasized in that debate the necessity for sound but easier money and for easier credit policy. I mentioned certain criticisms of the governor, of his alleged restrictionist ideas on these matters. In that debate I begged the
Governor of Bank of Canada government to tell us what were their views on those matters, to clear up the confusion and resolve any conflict, if there was one, not only between the government and the governor but between ministers inside the government. I begged them to tell us on this side and to tell the House of Commons who was responsible for what. My own view was clear. The minister has put it on the record and I am glad to repeat it:
It the governor cannot agree with the general policy which the government desires him to implement, then the governor has no alternative, of course, but to resign.
But after an inquiry into the accusation made against him, and only then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition did not say that on February 21.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is simple elementary justice; it may be strange to some of my hon. friends opposite who talk so much about parliamentary justice and rights. I went on to say that if the governor operated in the field of monetary policy without any indication of government disapproval, the governor then has surely the right to assume that the government supports the policy he is putting forward. The evidence of the minister's statements-and I have quoted some of them- shows that they did support that policy even though they attack it so bitterly now. Look at the speech made in Toronto on January 11, 1960, by the new crusader for expansionist finance, when he talked about the difficult decisions that had to be made in 1959, and I quote; "in the cause of steady rather than explosive and inflationary progress". He added, as found at page 2 of the text of his speech:
Our concern today is not whether we will continue to grow but what kind of growth we wish and will have.
Was that Coyne or Fleming speaking? Well, it was both. The minister went on:
Too often we have been tempted to pursue too rapid a rate of growth with too little regard for the inevitable consequences.
Was that the governor or the minister speaking? Listen to this. It will be found in the same speech:
It was not yet a time-
This was 1959.
-for a severe application of fiscal restraint, but the situation did require a reduction in the stimulus which government fiscal policies had injected into the economic stream.
And so he went on. He said we must avoid:
expenditures not strictly necessary now and bring government revenue and expenditures into better balance.
This was the minister, the restrictionist. What about the banks? What did he have

Governor of Bank of Canada to say about the banks in those days? Well, in his speech in Toronto he indicated that he was pleased because:
The restraints imposed by the chartered banks on the growth of over-all bank credit and their more selective policy of lending appears to have brought about a more orderly situation within the banking system.
Part of the same speech reads as follows:
Credit restrictions continue to impose difficulties for certain sections of the economy although there is no evidence that from the over-all viewpoint they are interfering with the process of growth.
Was this the governor of the Bank of Canada? No, this was the Minister of Finance speaking in January, 1960.
The expansionist.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will quote more from his restrictionist speeches. He said in the same speech in 1960:
We are seeking deliberately to bring our revenues and expenditures into closer balance in order that we may not find it necessary to make new borrowings.
In the same speech in Toronto he concluded as follows:
Those who practice thrift are entitled to the reward of the protection of their savings against the ravages of inflation. X shall continue to do all that lies within my power as Minister of Finance to encourage and protect the savings of the people, however small.
If Canadians can hold production costs in line and demonstrate renewed efficiency as producers and salesmen, and if they are prepared to take the self-denying measures needed to resist the lurking dangers of inflation, the present period of expansion could carry the Canadian economy far beyond the high water marks heretofore attained.
Then, a year later at Brantford, in January, 1961, in words that could have come from the governor himself, in words that make a mockery of the present attempt to pin on the governor, the blame for tight money and restrictionist policies the minister had this to say about the money supply:
The chartered banks are in a strong and improved position compared with a year ago. Their total assets increased during 1960 by approximately $750 million, or 6 per cent. Over the same 12-month period the total money supply increased by $687 million, or a little more than 5 per cent. During the year the general loans of the chartered banks increased by $275 million, or 6 per cent, and the ramainder of the increase in their total assets was reflected in the rise of more than $475 million (or 12 per cent) in their liquid and quickly marketable assets. This included, in addition to a rise in their cash, day to day loans and treasury bills, an increase of $260 million in their holdings of government bonds, and their net foreign assets have risen by $100 million.-
The minister who now condemns the governor of the Bank of Canada because he was a restrictionist in those days, went on to say:
In other words, the Canadian banking system has increased its loans during 1960 without strain on its liquid position; in fact it has added to its

liquidity and is in a position to meet all reasonable borrowing requirements of credit-worthy businesses and institutions.
The minister used those words, but Mr. Coyne certainly could have used them at that time. That was the policy in 1960, and its virtues were sung-
Just a few months ago.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The speech was made in 1961. The virtues of the policy were sung repeatedly by both the minister and the governor in other speeches.
In following these principles of that day the minister had a goal which he reaches, he thought, in last year's budget, which has now been repudiated by him though apparently it has not been repudiated by the governor of the Bank of Canada with whom he shared the desire to reach it last year. And yet now the minister complains that the governor and the government have become incompatible. "The government's policy" the minister says "is expansionist-the policies advocated by Mr. Coyne are restrictionist". Well, of course, some of the governor's policies are, but so are many of the things advocated by the minister in his earlier budgets. His 1960 budget, he admitted himself, was a stand-pat one. His baby budget of last December was hardly better. It was certainly not one to which the governor of the Bank of Canada could object. Expansionism, apart from some proposals in the 1958 budget as bait for the 1958 election, has been conspicuous by its absence in government policy during a time of recession when it was most needed. Yet we are now told that this was the basis of the government's difference with the governor of the Bank of Canada, a difference which is very hard to detect in the budget of this year. Mr. Bruce Macdonald, writing in the Globe and Mail of June 20, had this to say:
So far as the outsider could tell, the government had come to accept the monetary approach laid down by Mr. Coyne, and the finance minister, the soul of orthodoxy, came to be regarded as his guardian angel.
I think that is quite enough, Mr. Speaker, though I could quote a lot of other things to demonstrate the hollow mockery of the ex post facto case that the governor of the Bank of Canada over all these years had been restrictionist while the government was expansionist and that finally they came to a parting of the ways and on May 30 the minister said: "We can go along no longer; you resign at once, or else".
In the face of this statement of the minister the governor says, in effect, that there is no question affecting bank policy or cooperation at issue between us and that the

bank has in fact always co-operated fully with respect to government policies and measures. He said this too:
At no time has the government expressed disagreement with the operations of the Bank of Canada under my management nor has there been any occasion on which the Bank of Canada has failed to co-operate... in support of government policy. I have never opposed government policy and do not wish to do so.
There is a statement from the minister which I have quoted and there is a statement from the governor which I have quoted and in the face of both these statements contradicting each other, in the face of a statement by a member of the board of directors contradicting what the minister has said today-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: -in the face of that situation the minister has the effrontery to stand up and say that he will not allow this matter to go before a committee of the House of Commons where the facts can be found and the truth ascertained. That is all we are asking. We are not supporting the governor. We are not supporting the governor's tactics.
What are you doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are on both sides of the fence as usual.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is not the issue before us.
All over the map.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We are the only party in this house that has criticized some of the things that the governor has put forward. Some of the things he has said and done have been good. Some of the things he has said and done have, according to our thinking, not been good for Canada. That is not the issue. The issue is simple decency and justice. The issue is whether a man in the high and responsible office of this man can be thrown out of his office by an act of parliament-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: He threw himself out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
-which does not give him the opportunity to face his accusers in a parliamentary committee. The high court of parliament, the House of Commons, is being asked to take action in this matter. We are asked to take as important a decision as the House of Commons can take, to discharge the governor of the Bank of Canada. We are being asked to do this without access to the facts except in so far as members of the government give us those facts. We are asked to do this before the man accused is given an opportunity to face those accusing him in a committee of the house which is being asked to take action. This is an intolerable position, and I suggest that even now the government will surely fall back on its own
Governor of Bank of Canada bill of rights-I should like to read it back to hon. members of the government again- and give this man the opportunity to be heard within the spirit of the bill of rights about which they boast so much. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), the following amendment:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this bill (C-114) be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce."

Mr. Speaker, I regret that, unlike the minister who introduced the bill and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), I have only a limited time. I had eight hours of material ready for this debate and the minister in introducing the bill supplied me with an additional eight hours of material. I should like to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition immediately on the excellence of his performance and the excellence of his arguments. I want to say at once that I have never heard him in better form. It is obvious that he read the headlines this morning in the Globe and Mail, as we all did, I am sure, and is doing his utmost to make a bid for the leadership of the new party which the Ontario young Liberals would like to see him do.
After looking at the bill before us and hearing the explanation of the minister I can only say in all sincerity, what arrogance and what a horrible insult to the intelligence of the Canadian voter his recitation was. When he sees fit to accuse the governor of the Bank of Canada, as he said, out of the tabloids of his memory, all I can ask in response to that is: Does this mean that his head is indeed made of stone because tabloids are inscribed on stone?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Tablets, not tabloids.

If the minister had not taken so long he would not have wound up with his neck stretched out nearly as far as it is for the opposition to hack off. The longer he talked, the longer his neck became. He even went to the extreme of attempting to take credit for the representations made to him a number of months ago in this regard by learned people in the university field. He forgets completely that they complained not of the attitudes of the governor of the Bank of Canada but rather they complained basically, as we also have complained, of the lack of co-operation that obviously has existed in this regard.

Governor of Bank of Canada I believe that the minister exposed his small stature and also the smallness of the government when, in a vain and desperate attempt to heap additional criticism by way of attack on the activities of the governor of the Bank of Canada, he complained about the use of paper belonging to the taxpayers and the use of a postage meter to which the governor of the bank had resorted in an attempt to defend the integrity of the office of governor and, indeed, the role of the Bank of Canada itself. I believe this was really hitting below the belt. We thought that the complaint about the pension plan was hitting way below the belt, but this complaint about the use of the postage meter is even lower than that.
I hope the Minister of Finance will remember that until royal assent has been given to the bill now before us-and in light of the number of trained seals that abound in this house I have no doubt that royal assent will eventually be given

the governor of the Bank of Canada is yet the governor of the Bank of Canada and is completely entitled to use whatever facilities are available to him to defend, as he sees fit, the integrity of the occupant of that office as well as the integrity of the institution itself.
I think the minister can fairly be accused of literally heaping piles of abuse on the governor of the bank while at the same time denying his right to reply before a committee of this house. The Minister of Finance was most vindictive in the whole of his speech and it is obvious that in this whole matter the government as usual has been playing it by ear and has proven itself to be quite deaf at that.
I find it very difficult to understand the minister's claim that he has defended the prestige of the Bank of Canada. I feel that it is very difficult at this stage to decide who is the more adequate defender of the prestige of the Bank of Canada, whether it is indeed the governor of the Bank of Canada or the Minister of Finance. I should like to call the minister's attention to a statement he made, and this is in line with a number of complaints he has had made recently, and again this morning, as recorded at page 2258 of Hansard of February 21, 1961:
Mr. Speaker, may I say that I have no right of censorship over the speeches of the governor of the Bank of Canada. He does not refer them to me. Why should he do so? This is a free country. He makes his own speeches and chooses his own themes.
The minister complains now that the governor of the Bank of Canada in fact did not consult him but made his own speeches on his own particular theme.
Before I go much further I should like to make our position perfectly clear. We believe that the Bank of Canada belongs to 

the people of Canada. We recognize that all of the shares are owned by the Minister of Finance on behalf of the people of Canada. We reiterate the basic position taken by the former governor, Mr. Towers, as well as by a former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley and other former ministers of finance, Mr. Abbott, and Mr. Dunning-and these expressions are all on record-that if there is a basic conflict of interest, or difference between the policies of the government and the head of the Bank of Canada, then the will of the owners of the bank, as expressed through the government of the day, must prevail.
We in this group appreciate at once that if the Conservative government is going to remain in office for any considerable length of time the continuation of Mr. Coyne in the office of governor is completely untenable. This has been admitted by Mr. Coyne himself in a number of releases which he has made since this issue has arisen. However, we also believe that to ask the parliament of Canada to approve of this bill without hearing before a committee of this parliament the accused man presenting his own case is an insult to the House of Commons itself. We in this group, therefore, intend to support with all the vigour at our command the amendment which has been put forward by the leader of the official opposition.
This is a battle in essence between the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada; the Minister of Finance versus Coyne. Which side of the coin is he on, or is he simply opposed? We have heard the minister speaking about devaluation of the coin of the realm. Is this a sign that the value of the coin of the realm is to prevail or is Mr. Coyne less dear?
We have also assumed that the basic philosophies in respect to monetary policies of the minister and of the governor were identical. We have always been led to believe so and, even at this late date, still think there is no fundamental difference between the basic approach of the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada. However, we now realize, after reading submissions made a number of months ago by the governor of the Bank of Canada to the Minister of Finance, that we have now arrived at a stage of socialism plus Tory policies rather than socialism versus free enterprise upon which ground the Prime Minister announced the next election campaign would be fought.
During the budget speech the Minister of Finance presented a number of projects recommended to him by the governor of the Bank of Canada, such as the vast expansion

of the industrial development bank. The governor of the Bank of Canada also encouraged, as the minister has so often done, an increase in savings by Canadian people, and he advocated a specific arrangement for a national development corporation. He also advocated the establishment of a local government finance corporation. I suggest we now have socialism plus private enterprise, and I should like to ask a question in all sincerity. Did Mr. Coyne indeed have a point of difference with the Minister of Finance when he pointed to the continuation of repeated attacks upon crown corporations, or does the government intend to pursue a policy of selling these crown corporations, thereby pursuing a policy of private profit versus a continuation of the very profitable crown corporations that we now have in Canada?
The governor of the Bank of Canada has repeatedly offered his co-operation. He claims, along with many other leading Canadians, that massive action on the part of the government is needed. I want to at least say this for him; although we may disagree with many of the measures he advocates, he has assumed responsibility for the welfare of Canada and Canadians, and has recommended to the government a program of massive action in order to meet the recession that we are now experiencing.
I should like to ask the minister, in light of the statements which he has made in regard to the governor of the Bank of Canada, where the basic difference lies. Despite the length of the minister's speech today he has not yet identified the real area of basic difference between himself and his policies and the governor of the Bank of Canada and his policies.
I realize the impracticality of the measures advocated by the governor of the Bank of Canada in the field of tariffs. I much prefer an honest proposal such as that made by the governor of the Bank of Canada in this field -even though I am very much opposed to it -to the back door method of raising tariffs that this government continually insists on pursuing.
The governor has called attention to the need for co-operation in the field of monetary and fiscal policy. This need was underlined by the standing committee on manpower of the other place. This need is becoming more obvious to many Canadians who have given any thought to the matter. I believe even the minister, in his announcement that a royal commission is to be appointed to examine the role of the Bank of Canada, is now admitting that there must be a tie-in between monetary and fiscal policies and that the minister is now admitting he was in error when he insisted that fiscal policies are the exclusive
Governor of Bank of Canada responsibility of government and monetary policies are the exclusive responsibility of the Bank of Canada and never need the twain necessarily meet. I think the minister is now definitely on the defensive on this score.
I should like to recall to the house what the governor of the Bank of Canada had to say in his submission to the government dated February 15 last:
Monetary policy undoubtedly has a part to play in any anti-recession economic program and also in fostering long term economic growth. Unfortunately very exaggerated views appear to be held in some quarters as to the degree to which monetary policy by itself can be effective for these purposes. There are several reasons why general monetary expansion, particularly if not tied in with government measures directly increasing production and employment, may not serve any useful purpose and may even have perverse effects opposite to those desired.
He added a little bit later:
-unless steps are taken in other fields of economic policy to ensure that increased spending by Canadians will direct itself to the purchase of goods and services produced in Canada, and thereby promote increased employment in Canada.
The governor of the bank also had this submission to make at page 3 of the same report:
The whole range of economic policy must be focused on the goals of promoting full employment and a satisfactory rate of economic growth without inflation, and restoration of equilibrium in the balance of payments.
He went on to say this:
It is urgently to be desired that a strong new initiative be undertaken, aimed directly at achieving increased production and employment in Canada.
This does not sound like the voice of a restrictionist. It sounds like the voice of an expansionist. Before the budget was brought down the minister asserted that he was the expansionist and that the governor of the Bank of Canada was the restrictionist. After listening to the budget it now appears that the minister is the restrictionist because in the budget there is hardly anything to substantiate his claim to being an expansionist; and it now appears that the governor of the Bank of Canada would not have opposed a deficit, even one of this size, if it was aimed at an expansionist policy. However, as I said before, we all know that the deficit is only because of some very poor housekeeping on the part of the government.
In his recommendations the governor of the Bank of Canada advocates the removal of the excise tax on automobiles; I refer to the excise tax of 7i per cent. The minister announces it in his budget. I see no basic conflict there. The governor goes a bit beyond the minister's announcement. He calls for measures to handle such difficulties as the lack of regional development. He advocates a national highways program much beyond

Governor of Bank of Canada that which is in existence today. The governor of the Bank of Canada especially underlines the need to develop effective demand on the part of Canadian consumers and he makes many recommendations whereby effective demand in the hands of consumers might be enhanced. He is much more expansionist in this regard than are the policies that have been recommended to this house by the Minister of Finance.
The governor of the Bank of Canada on February 15 last recommended the establishment of a secondary mortgage market. We have since heard that this idea has now been adopted by the government. He recommends that our dollar on the international market be regulated. The only conflict I can see is that the policies of the Minister of Finance leave the potential value of the Canadian dollar very much in doubt. We do not know whether it is going to be discounted at 5 per cent next week, at 15 per cent or at any percentage. The recommendation of the governor of the Bank of Canada was that it be given a definite and fixed rate of exchange and that it be maintained at par with the United States dollar. We therefore fail to see very much of a basic conflict between the policies that have been adopted by the government and the policies that have been advocated by the governor of the Bank of Canada.
This morning we heard a long harangue. First of all, we had the crocodile tears shed on behalf of the personal welfare of Mr. Coyne. I believe that in the long run of things the Minister of Finance ought to be worried more about his own potential welfare in the years to come than about the welfare of the governor of the Bank of Canada. He said there is no personal element involved. Yet in all the releases I have read from the governor of the Bank of Canada there has been a lack of involvement of personalities. That is something that we certainly could not say for the speech of the minister of this morning. It was merely a diatribe attacking the integrity of the governor of the Bank of Canada. He complains of the attack of the governor on himself.
I believe that all the minister and the government are really worried about is that, after the governor of the Bank of Canada was made completely aware of the intentions of this government, he outmanoeuvred them, he outsmarted them at every turn, that he is now ending up on the top of the heap and the government finds itself on the short end of the stick and they are regretting it; and therefore, as the only way out in a desperate move, they are attempting to attack the integrity of the governor himself. How else can we explain the government's suddenly

waking up to the fact after 16 long months have elapsed, that an increase has been allowed to the pension of the governor, despite the fact that the minister had the assistant deputy minister in attendance at this meeting 16 long months ago? The Canadian people will regard this only as a smokescreen.
The minister complains that confidential documents have now suddenly been released to the public. Did the minister expect that a responsible officer, the leading officer of the Bank of Canada, was going to allow his office to be dragged through the political mud from the Atlantic to the Pacific and that he would remain bound by that promise that all exchanges would1 remain confidential? Certainly in what the minister told us this morning he revealed many of the confidential discussions that had taken place. I contend the only complaint is that hon. gentlemen opposite are smarting under the ability of the governor of the Bank of Canada to outmanoeuvre them. This was something they had not expected. As I said before, they were so inflated with their arrogance that they did not think a civil servant would have the guts to fight back and defend his rights, much as I disagree and much as my group disagrees with many of the ideas that have been submitted over the past number of years by the governor.
There is another matter I wish to mention. The minister was asked the other day whether the international monetary fund people had been consulted on the proposal to tamper with the value of the Canadian dollar. The minister replied, in effect, that he could not be sure; Mr. Rasminsky, who is a deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, had been in New York on the day the budget was presented and he may have had discussions with the officials of the international monetary fund.
Mr. Speaker, we must consider this in the light of the minister's claim that the governor of the bank himself has not been consulted about the contents of the budget. The minister was very firm in making that claim. The minister inadvertently admitted that he has been consulting, regarding the contents of the budget before its release in this house, whom, if you please, but the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada; but he did not deem it advisable to consult with the governor of the Bank of Canada himself. I say this because unless Mr. Rasminsky had knowledge of the proposals contained in the budget, he would have been in no position to discuss these proposals on Tuesday last with officials of the international monetary fund. The minister really opened his flanks on that score, and it is one more clear indication that the minister over the past number of years, as it

now becomes obvious, has made very little, if any, effort to work in harness with the governor of the Bank of Canada.
The minister claims that he gave the governor every opportunity to go with dignity. What a farce this claim becomes when the minister himself admits that one of the five things he discussed with the governor when he asked him to resign was the issue of his pension arrangements, which had been settled by unanimous decision of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada as far back as 16 months previously.
How do you claim that you are asking a man to go with dignity when 16 months after the event, and after the minister's officials knew of this event, you raise this as a matter for discussion? The minister admits that the governor of the Bank of Canada asked for an hour to think it over. I want to compliment the governor of the Bank of Canada. He did not immediately rise in wrath, as the minister so often does in this House of Commons. He considered that his basic integrity had been attacked, but he at least asked for an hour to cool off, to think it over and to come back with a suitable reply. I think this is a procedure the minister himself might adopt on many occasions in this House of Commons and not be so perfectly ready to interject with "utter nonsense" and words of that kind.
The minister complains that the governor of the bank released confidential information to the Canadian public on June 13 last. The governor on that day knew and had already been informed that the arms of the directors of the Bank of Canada had been twisted and that very same evening they would be asking for the governor's resignation. All I can say is that the government have raised a phony issue here and their basic resentment is that they were outmanoeuvred by the governor of the Bank of Canada.
The minister says that parliament must decide who governs this country. I contend that parliament must also decide whether or not we get all the facts, and up till now it is obvious that we have not received the facts. To say that parliament must decide, in the light of the lack of the facts, is merely to say, "we will use our rubber stamp majority in order to enforce our will in this regard". The minister says:
We will not accept responsibility for the governor and his actions when we have lost all confidence in him.
I would like to ask the minister how this happens to square with all his indications over the years that he has complete confidence in the Bank of Canada to determine monetary policy. The minister complains that the governor of the Bank of Canada had been requested to ease the tight money policy in
Governor of Bank of Canada the winter of 1957-58. I would like to ask the minister, how does this square with his continuous pledge to the House of Commons that he dare not interfere in the determination of monetary policy? Now today, at long last, he admits to us that he attempted indeed to interfere in the activities of the Bank of Canada as far back as 1957 and 1958.
I believe that the only complaint against the governor, as recited by the minister, in 1958 was the governor's action in releasing the annual report of the bank at the normal time because it was politically embarrassing to the government. This, in the eyes of the minister, was most reprehensible. Apparently he expected the governor of the Bank of Canada to consider the political fortunes of a political party over and beyond his responsibilities and his duty as governor of the Bank of Canada.
I feel this admission on the part of the government was most regrettable. They complain about that matter although the governor performed his functions in a proper manner. It happened to be unfortunate, I will grant, for the government of the day to have the annual report of the Bank of Canada released at that time. However the unpardonable sin of the governor of the Bank of Canada was that he performed his responsibility and released the annual report of 1957 in 1958, at the time this report is normally released. It happened to be embarrassing for the government, and therefore Mr. Coyne's head must roll.
The minister admitted that perhaps the government should have asked for the resignation of Mr. Coyne a long time ago. We agree with this wholeheartedly. If we are to believe the statements the minister has made in the last week or two, the government has shown itself to be utterly derelict in its responsibility to the people of Canada in not asking for the resignation of the governor. However if we are to believe the statement made by the minister over the years in regard to the activities of the governor of the Bank of Canada, the only conclusion we can come to regarding why now the government suddenly claim he is the evil influence on Canadian prosperity that they contend is that an election may be drawing nigh and they have to attempt to blame somebody else for their own lack of action over the past four years.
The minister agrees that it is up to the House of Commons to decide when the governor has to go. The governor himself has admitted that he ought to go if and when there is a basic conflict of attitude between the governor of the bank and the government of the day. But the minister today has not

Governor of Bank of Canada produced any evidence that such a basic conflict exists. I recommend that hon. members read the statement of the governor of the bank submitted on February 15 last. In the main his prescription to end unemployfnent in Canada is not very far removed from many of the statements made recently by the Minister of Finance himself. The minister says this question should be left for the house to decide. I want to warn this government that though the matter might well be left to this house-and I have no doubt the house will likely go along with the government in reaching a decision-there is an even higher court than this parliament, namely, the court of the people. This smokescreen about the release of confidential documents, which is of more recent origin, is not going to work. The Canadian electorate today has gone beyond grades 1, 2 and 3. I believe the Canadian electorate will realize that this is nothing but a smokescreen. There is such a thing as character assassination. We contend that there has been nothing else, in essence, but character assassination in this issue. In no circumstances do we endorse a pension of $25,000 a year for any man in Canada. But let us not forget that this is not the responsibility of the governor of the bank. This was done by the unanimous decision of a Tory appointed board of directors of the Bank of Canada. If the minister is now able to twist the arms of the directors in order to persuade them to get rid of Mr. Coyne, how much easier would it have been for him 16 months ago when this pension issue arose to have twisted their arms and prevented this increase in pension being provided for a man who is supposed to be the retiring governor of the Bank of Canada.
The minister himself admits there is a need for the integration of fiscal and financial policies, but he has had to confess there was no consultation with the governor of the bank on the basically valuable submissions-I say this though I am not in agreement with them -made in the field of economic policy by the governor of the bank to the government on February 15 last.
I think the government imagined they could get away with it by going to the voters and carrying on an appeal against the bankers and those terrible people who increase their own pensions from $12,000 to $25,000 a year.
I take the view that the Canadian people support fair play and believe that every man should be heard in court. Therefore we take great pleasure in endorsing the amendment which was moved by the leader of the official opposition.

I watched the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) taking part the other night in a conference on television. My impression from what he said was that he intended to drop Mr. Coyne like a hot potato. I think the hon. gentleman's speech here this afternoon has borne out that impression. He has dropped the governor of the Bank of Canada like a hot potato. Not one logical argument did he put forward why Mr. Coyne should not be fired by act of parliament. Not one argument did he bring forward why we should not proceed with this bill. I noticed no one questions whether or not Mr. Coyne should go. It is obvious to all that there has been a disagreement between the government and the governor of the bank, and in that situation the Leader of the Opposition and everyone else in this house agrees that the government should stay and not Mr. Coyne. The Leader of the Opposition went on to say that before Mr. Coyne leaves his post-before he leaves his barricades in the Bank of Canada -we should have a committee of the House of Commons inquire into the situation. The hon. gentleman says that under the bill of rights Mr. Coyne has the right to appear before a committee of parliament to state his case. He says that the bill of rights which was established to provide for the liberty of the subject, should keep Mr. Coyne from taking his liberty at the earliest possible date.
The question of Mr. Coyne's pension has been introduced. That is not germane to the particular question at issue. That is not the reason he was asked to resign, but certainly it is worthy of consideration by this house that the governor of the Bank of Canada in preparing for the conclusion of his term in office in December of this year should have made arrangements for a pension equivalent to that paid to former presidents of the United States, a pension which is some $22,000 greater than that received by the last prime minister of Canada. Of course, that is not the reason why Mr. Coyne was asked to take his leave, but it does indicate something of the nature of Mr. Coyne, something of his arrogance, something about what he himself, at any rate, thinks he is worth to this nation.
Why should there be an inquiry into this request that Mr. Coyne submit his resignation? The issue is a simple one. In the case of a disagreement between the Minister of Finance who speaks on matters of finance for the people of Canada, and Mr. Coyne, it is the governor who goes and not the minister of finance. That is in accordance with our parliamentary system. The only question before the house today is whether there has been a disagreement, whether the minister feels he

can no longer work with Mr. Coyne. If that question is answered in the affirmative, the bill should be passed without a dissenting vote.
Both the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member who has just taken his seat agree that Mr. Coyne has no right to remain in office after being asked to resign, but they say he does have the right to appear before a parliamentary committee to state his case. It seems to me that the reasons are very clear why Mr. Coyne has to go. His statements were on many occasions contradictory to those of the Minister of Finance. It was obvious for all to see that Mr. Coyne did not agree with the fiscal policies of this government which he criticized from time to time. It is obvious there was sufficient difference there to justify the Minister of Finance in coming before this house and asking for a replacement.
Mr. Coyne is a man who stands for high tariffs, isolationism, ultra-protectionism. He seems to find in these policies the answer to Canadian employment and economic difficulties. He attacks deficit budgets, both federal and provincial, which would release more money to provide more purchasing power for our people and, above all, give us the opportunity which has been taken by the Minister of Finance in the budget, to stimulate those areas of the economy which need stimulating. Mr. Coyne's way is to increase taxes. Mr. Coyne's way is to disregard our international agreements, to raise tariffs and shut out goods of other nations. His way is to ride roughshod across agreements we have made with other countries of the world and to interfere with the movement of goods across international boundaries. The policy of this government has been entirely the opposite of that. It may well be that Mr. Coyne has the same purpose in mind as the present government but his proposed methods are entirely different.
This government has been working for four years to stimulate the economy of Canada. Policies have been brought forward to encourage the use of Canadian money in Canada, to encourage investment of Canadian funds in Canada. During the past winter we saw a trade conference called by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to try to speed up the sales of Canadian goods throughout the world. We have seen the vocational training legislation brought forward so that the young people of Canada who badly need new skills, mav obtain the ability to run the machines of our modern community. The government's desire is to give them that training. We have seen the special effort to sell
Governor of Bank of Canada agricultural products and we have noted particularly the tremendous success of the Minister of Agriculture in placing large orders with the republic of China. We have seen the development of our forestry industry. All of these moves have been purposed to stimulate the Canadian economy. All in this parliament, I am sure, like this government, want to stimulate the Canadian economy but not by ultraprotectionism, not by the inflexibility of interest rates, not by isolationism and anti-Americanism.
It is obvious to all of us that the conflict between the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada had to do with fiscal policy. Indeed, it has been asked what authority or what business the governor of the Bank of Canada had in going across the nation to weaken the work of a government which has been attempting to stimulate the economy of Canada. His position has been that if it will not be done my way it will not be done at all. This is the reason parliament is being asked today to declare a vacancy in the governorship in the Bank of Canada.
Every effort has been made in this budget to stimulate and aid the automobile industry by reducing the 7-J per cent sales tax. The whole economy will be helped by the decision to lower the rate of exchange on the Canadian dollar as against the United States dollar. This is a decision which would have been opposed by Mr. Coyne.
The Minister of Finance put up with Mr. Coyne as long as he could. He did everything he could to try to avoid a public quarrel with the governor of the Bank of Canada, to try to keep from open conflict which he knew would occur if he asked the governor of the Bank of Canada to resign. However, when this budget was to be introduced with its special accent on the development of the Canadian economy, the minister knew that Mr. Coyne could very well step back on the hustings, as he has been doing in the last few years, to attack the budget and the policies of the government.
In his very small argument on behalf of the governor of the Bank of Canada the Leader of the Opposition raised very few points. First he said there should be an inquiry. An inquiry into what? To illustrate the thing that is most obvious to all Canadians, namely that Mr. Coyne differed very widely from the Minister of Finance? He said the bill should not be brought forward and should not be passed by this house because no reasons are given in the bill for asking that the governorship be made vacant. Well, sufficient reasons have been supplied even

Governor of Bank of Canada up to this time in this debate to show the Leader of the Opposition why this bill should be passed.
Then there is the very weak argument that Mr. Coyne after all is being charged as a criminal and should have the right to come before the courts to defend himself. No one is taking anything from Mr. Coyne that infringes upon his liberty. No one is discriminating against him because of his colour or his creed. How can the bill of rights apply in the matter of a public servant who finds that he cannot agree with the government of the day and who in his arrogance refuses to resign at the request of the representative of the people of Canada?
Another argument the Leader of the Opposition made was that if Mr. Coyne should be fired he should have been fired long ago. Many hon. members might agree that Mr. Coyne should have disappeared from the public scene long ago; that he has done harm to Canada in the speeches he made, in the policies he advocated, particularly when he spoke from a position which would lead the people to think that he spoke for the government of Canada. But the reason put forward by the Minister of Finance I am sure will indicate to every hon. member that he made every attempt possible to prevent a public quarrel with Mr. Coyne, and indeed only asked for his resignation as a last resort, because his removal is necessary to the measures proposed by the budget.
Last Friday, I believe it was, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), in speaking in the budget debate, raised questions with regard to the dismissal of Mr. Coyne, or the request for his resignation. Then he gave the house a list of the names of people who for one reason or another had resigned or retired from the public service and he attempted to argue that these people were fired from their positions; that the government was persecuting people in the public service. He suggested that the men whose names he listed were people who had been ousted from their jobs on government demand. He mentioned Mr. Hector McKinnon, chairman of the tariff board. Mr. McKinnon retired some three years ago at age 70. He certainly retired of his own volition; there was no question of his being asked to leave his post. I might say also that since then Mr. McKinnon has been working for the government and at the moment he is chief negotiator at Geneva where the GATT agreement is under negotiation.
