Mention was also made of Mr. Clarence Shepard, the former chief commissioner of the board of transport commissioners. Mr. Shepard also left of his own volition to take up an occupation which he felt would be


much more profitable. He is now vice president of British American Oil of Toronto.
The hon. member also referred to Mr. George Mclvor, chief commissioner of the Canadian wheat board. Mr. Mclvor retired from the wheat board because of age and for no other reason. He certainly retired of his own volition.
Reference was made to Mr. Davidson Dunton, formerly chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C. It was well known to every member of this house that Mr. Dunton retired from the chairmanship of the board of the C.B.C. only because he much preferred a post he was offered as president of Carleton university.
The hon. member also referred to Mr. Ernest Bushnell, general manager of the C.B.C. who retired some time ago. I am sure that every hon. member, except the hon. member for Leeds, knows full well that Mr. Bushnell left the C.B.C. to set up the private T.V. station CJOH, Ottawa, which is certainly a much more profitable occupation than continuing in his work with the C.B.C.
Mr. L. H. Nicholson, formerly commissioner of the R.C.M.P. was mentioned. He retired from the R.C.M.P. after a difference with the Minister of Justice, as he ought to have done. This was a question on which the commissioner and the minister could not agree. Mr. Nicholson retired because he could not agree with the minister and his department, but he did not attempt to challenge the authority of the minister, the department and of the public of Canada as Mr. Coyne seeks to do.
Mr. Mitchell Sharp, former deputy minister of the Department of Trade and Commerce, also left of his own volition. Mr. William Buchanan of the tariff board left that board to establish himself in Ottawa as a tariff consultant and I am sure he would very much prefer to continue in that work than in his former post. Mr. Alan H. Jarvis, director of the national art gallery, left for reasons quite clear to everyone in the House of Commons. Mr. Charles Gavsie, of the St. Lawrence seaway, left the St. Lawrence seaway to become a partner in a Montreal law firm. Mr. Jean Lessard, of the St. Lawrence seaway, left that post to become chairman of the Quebec hydro.
In all of these cases, which are routine cases, men who were in the public service and who had received valuable training in the public service left to take up work which was more lucrative or which gave them a wider field for their abilities. It is the type of thing that always goes on in the public

service and none of these situations are tantamount to the request that was made to Mr. Coyne for his resignation.
As a matter of fact, far from the charge of the member for Leeds that the government is persecuting senior civil servants and public servants, everyone in the house is quite aware of the work that the government has done to restore civil servants to their proper position in the nation. The new Civil Service Act, which will shortly be before the house, is the first legislation in 43 years to improve the position of the civil service and the civil servants of Canada. It sets up negotiation procedures, grievance procedures, appeal procedures and so on which have been requested by the civil service for many a year. Needless to say, their words fell upon deaf ears for many years before 1957.
The Leader of the Opposition said there should be an inquiry. It is rumoured around the house today that this Bank of Canada debate could well take four or five days. Who is this proud man who refuses to accept the invitation of the Minister of Finance to resign? Who is this man who says he will not accept the will of the elected representatives of the people and says he will take his case over our heads to the people of Canada? Who is this prima donna of the Bank of Canada who would tie up this house for four or five days and then ask that in addition an inquiry should be conducted before a standing committee to go into a matter which is already obvious and clear to the Canadian people?
I am sure that there has been no more arrogant man upon the Canadian scene in many years than this man who refuses to resign and insists upon asking parliament to take up its time, when we have so much legislation before us necessary for the stimulation of the Canadian economy, to deal with his case alone. If this debate lasts four days or if it lasts 24 days, I venture to say there will be no member of the House of Commons who will get up and say that he is sorry to see Mr. Coyne go. I venture to say there will be no member of the House of Commons who will arise to say that Mr. Coyne should not have resigned when asked to do by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes, there will be. There is one right here.
And lots more.
I am glad to hear that Mr. Coyne has one friend in the House of Commons because up to now there has been very little argument put forward to support him.

That is not the issue.
Governor of Bank of Canada

Certainly as far as I am concerned I am prepared to support the bill and I am sure that most members of parliament will be glad to see this post in the Bank of Canada become vacant and a successor to Mr. Coyne appointed. The work of the nation must go on. Who is this man who will hold it up because he refuses to do what any other man would do in the same situation and yield to the constitutional privileges of the Minister of Finance and of the parliament of Canada?
Indeed, it has certainly come as a surprise to me to see so many members of the C.C.F. party rallying to the support of Mr. Coyne, although such support will not go so far, I am sure, as to say that this man should succeed and the people of Canada should fail. It is startling to hear that members of the C.C.F. party, who always pose as the champions of justice in the house, feel that Mr. Coyne after 6j years in office is entitled to a pension of the type he has provided for himself. It is startling to hear that they are supporting a man whose policy, uttered many times across the nation, is against deficit financing at a time when more work could thereby be provided for people who are unemployed in the nation. It is interesting to hear members of the C.C.F. party rising to support a man who champions high interest rates and inflexibility in exchange rates.
It will be interesting to hear members of the Liberal party, who have always pretended to assume a position against high tariffs, rise to support this man who is the proponent of arbitrary high tariffs. I doubt very much, as I have said, if anyone will be sincerely sorry to see Mr. Coyne go. Indeed, I know that all members of the house agree that when a conflict arises between the government of this nation and the governor of the Bank of Canada, no matter how majestic the governor has made himself he should retire before the will of the people.

Mr. Speaker, the principle involved in the discussion before us is not complicated. No one, I think, will deny its importance. Therefore I am a little surprised that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) should not have been supported today by some of his ministerial colleagues, particularly by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Give him time.

I can only suspect that the Prime Minister has not taken part in the debate and has not been in the house this afternoon because of preoccupations involving the Prime Minister of Japan. But it

Governor of Bank of Canada is inconceivable that in a matter of this importance the ministerial benches should not have been filled and that evidence should not have been given by the ministry and by the Conservative party as a whole of a deep interest in this matter. Instead, we have had a statement by the Minister of Finance and now one by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan).
I must say I am amazed that a young member of parliament of the quality of the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond should have been guilty of some of the statements he made in the course of his speech this afternoon, particularly some of the questions that he put to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). Among those questions were: Why should the Leader of the Opposition plead for the right of the governor of the Bank of Canada to be heard? Why should the Leader of the Opposition urge this house to give to someone who opposed the Minister of Finance the opportunity of replying in another forum to arguments put forward today by the Minister of Finance in the exercise of what the hon. member said were the constitutional prerogatives of the Minister of Finance, whatever they may be?
I say to the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond that he cannot have followed clearly what the Leader of the Opposition said. I can only say that the hon. member has not fully understood the meaning of the phrase, rule of law. He has not fully understood what we mean by due process of law. He has not understood the implications in the mischievous bills of attainder of the Tudor period. He has not understood how Hitler dispensed justice by totalitarian methods without giving opportunity of reply to the accused. He has not understood the meaning of the energies and the exploits of Patrick Henry.
The hon. gentleman said, why should this house be put to the inconvenience of a five-day inquiry?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Terrible.

Has the hon. gentleman not understood that justice is something that cannot be confronted with the argument of inconvenience? Would the hon. member not be the first to rise in his place and defend the right of any accused, notwithstanding the inconvenience to which it might put any individual member of the house, whether it be a member of the government, whether it be a member supporting the government or a member in the opposition groups to make a defence of his position? If there is a violation of justice of any kind under our system of law and our form of government no man should be denied the opportunity of having his full day in


court. That is the gist of the plea made today by the Leader of the Opposition.
Does the hon. member for Invemess-Rich-mond not recall the words of the bill of rights which he so strongly supported last year, that bill of rights which provides in section 2, as the Leader of the Opposition reminded us, that no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to deprive a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations?
If the bill of rights is now to guarantee to one charged with a violation of the Criminal Code the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of justice, is the governor of the Bank of Canada, who has not violated our criminal law but who has simply disagreed with the policies of this government, to have less than that which is provided in that guarantee of the bill of rights for one who violates the Criminal Code?
The bill of rights also provides that no law of Canada shall be so construed or applied so as to deprive a person charged with an offence of the right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty according to law. The hon. gentleman I am sure in his studies is aware of the common law right of the citizen to be presumed innocent until found guilty, a presumption which, not without some effort, we in the Liberal party last year were able to have incorporated in the bill of rights.
Is this presumption of innocence to be accorded to a criminal, yet denied an important servant of the government of Canada? That is the issue in this particular situation, and it is one to which we have not had the Minister of Finance address himself.
The Minister of Finance comes in with a meagre bill asking this house to declare vacant a post which comes into existence as a result of a decision taken by the directors of the Bank of Canada, subject to the governor in council. These directors act under the authority given them in the Bank of Canada Act, yet we are now asked to declare this post vacant and to accept in substantiation of that plea of the Minister of Finance not the written evidence of the accused as well as the submissions of the prosecutor, but ex parte statements of the Minister of Finance made in the absence of the governor of the Bank of Canada, without giving him the opportunity of putting his side of the case before this house.
Oh, oh.

The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) now seems to express some disagreement with me. I should remind that hon. gentleman, one of the younger members of this house, of his proud boast that one of the reasons he came into this chamber was because he could add his voice to the defence of freedom and our concept of the rule of law. Here is the opportunity for that hon. gentleman, with his whole future before him, to say to the government, I do not agree with what the governor of the Bank of Canada has done, nor with his policies, because I do not believe there can be two sovereignties in our country-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

-but where a man is charged by one side and not given the opportunity to put his case forward then I must say, on the basis of an appreciation of what is often called ordinary British justice, I am going to fight for the right of that man at least to have his day in court. We are not getting that kind of support from the hon. gentleman. The two hon. gentlemen I have singled out are two young members of the Conservative party, and they should be among the first to join with the Leader of the Opposition in the plea that he has made today.
When I said a moment ago there could not be two sovereignties in this country the Minister of Finance applauded that statement. I should like the minister to know that this is not the first time I have made that statement in this house. I made that statement-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On March 22.

I made that statement on March 22 and I repeat it today. I have always taken the position, as has the Leader of the Opposition, that there is no room in this country for two sovereignties and that where there is a difference between a leading official in the public service and the government of the day there can be no public disagreement unless that disagreement is concurred in by the administration. We in this party have always stood for that principle. We have complained about the position taken publicly by the governor of the Bank of Canada, and no one has taken a stronger position in that regard than I have myself, and I am not afraid to defend that position. That is not what confronts us now.
When we argued that the governor of the Bank of Canada had publicly taken a position different from the government of the day in matters of fiscal policy in areas outside the monetary field, the Minister of Finance at no time indicated in this house, as the Leader
Governor of Bank of Canada of the Opposition pointed out, until very recently, that there was any disagreement between the governor of the Bank of Canada and himself. We were told this morning for the first time of a situation that eventuated in 1957-58. The Minister of Finance as a result of that admission today stands indicted by his own words. If that was the situation three and a half years ago the government of this country, and particularly the Minister of Finance should have taken the step, but taken it in circumstances that would not have destroyed or weakened the confidence which the Canadian people and people outside in other countries should have in our financial institutions, including the Bank of Canada. That is the situation that confronts us now.
We have asked repeatedly in this house for the right to examine the governor of the Bank of Canada on these statements in areas outside the field of monetary policy, a field in which, under the Bank of Canada Act, he is given the power of formulation and direction. That does not mean, of course, as we have heard repeatedly argued, that the government has not a responsibility in that field as well. We have taken the position, and we reiterate this position, that the government of Canada is responsible for policies laid down by any agency of government in our country. No government, unless it wants to abdicate its functions and abdicate its responsibility, could take any other position. In the field of monetary policy, this has always been done as was pointed out by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) a few moments ago in respect of the position of the Minister of Finance of Canada. That was the position taken by Mr. Charles Dunning when he said:
A long continuance of a policy that conflicts with the government view becomes impossible.
That was the position taken by Mr. Ilsley when he said:
The monetary policy which the bank carries out from time to time must be the government's monetary policy.
That was the policy of Mr. Abbott when he said:
The ultimate responsibility must fall upon the government.
That was the policy of Mr. Harris when he said:
The government is satisfied ... that... it was desirable to moderate the rate of monetary expansion.
The Minister of Finance is the only minister of finance who takes a different view. I compare what the minister has said now with what Mr. Rhodes said, in 1934 when the Bank of Canada Act was introduced in this house by the Conservative government, that

Governor of Bank of Canada the government has no authority in the field of monetary policy, because he has forgotten that, as a private member of this house in the banking and commerce committee, the member for Eglinton of that day, now the Minister of Finance, said the minister of finance had a very direct responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was before 1957-58.

There can be no doubt as to the position of the government in relation to the Bank of Canada in the field of monetary policy. If the governor of the Bank of Canada had at any time formulated a monetary policy which was in disagreement with the views of the government, the course was clear. It was clear it was the duty of the government, in such circumstances, to make that position clear to the governor. From what the present governor has said and from what the former governor has said we know that in such circumstances there would be no alternative but for the governor of the Bank of Canada to resign. But there is no question of such disagreement here in this particular situation between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the government on monetary policy. That is not the issue before us.
We learned only a few days ago from the Minister of Finance that it was only on May 30 that the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada profoundly disagreed in those areas outside of the governor's specific legislative authority, namely, in fiscal and financial matters and that there was a disagreement between the governor and himself. He says today that there was disagreement away back in 1957-58. I repeat that was the time for the Minister of Finance to act in accordance with what are erroneously called the constitutional prerogatives of the Minister of Finance.
This question of the responsibility of the government in the matter of monetary policy is important in this discussion. We have had circulated today two letters, one dated June 9 and one dated June 26, signed by the present governor of the Bank of Canada and addressed to the Minister of Finance. I want to comment on these two letters in supporting the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition today, that this whole matter can be satisfactorily disposed of only by full opportunity being given for the full disclosure of all the facts. The Minister of Finance cannot, in all fairness, take the position that he alone is in a position fully, fairly and objectively, to disclose the facts.
We have here before us the letter of the governor of the Bank of Canada of June 9.

I think it is important that some excerpts from this letter be placed on Hansard at this time. In the second paragraph of this letter the governor of the Bank of Canada states:
On this last point I have expressed the view frequently, and I have no doubt this has been reported to you, that the relationship of the bank to the government should be clarified and the overriding responsibility for monetary policy declared to rest on the government (as it always has done in fact) by appropriate provision in the statute. Lord Cobbold, the governor of the Bank of England, on his last visit here told me, and perhaps you also, that the provisions to that effect in the Bank of England act carried his complete support and did not in his view derogate from the operating independence of the Bank of England or from its status as an entity separate from the government and with a responsibility of its own, although in certain circumstances the governor of the bank might find himself in such fundamental disagreement with government policy as communicated to him that (unlike a civil servant) he would find it necessary to resign, no doubt giving reasons for his resignation and allowing those reasons to become the subject of public information and discussion.
We were not told anything about this by the Minister of Finance. We were not told that the governor had explained to him, as he explains in this letter of June 9, what his position was with regard to resignations in the matter of a disagreement in the context as visualized by Lord Cobbold and by the governor of the bank himself in this letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That letter I said was received on June 12.
My friend said there was a letter but he did not tell us what was in that letter.
He concealed it from parliament.

He did not tell us that, any more than he told us what was in the letter of Mr. Bryden about which I am going to have something to say. We have not heard anything of this story yet. If the Minister of Finance wishes to create in the minds of the people of this country the confidence that he should promote as Minister of Finance, he should be the first to assist us in the fullest exposition of all of the dirty circumstances involved in this matter.
I stand here and I fully except the charge made by the Minister of Finance that in the industrial relations committee I had taken issue with the governor of the Bank of Canada and, I learn now for the first time, in such a manner as to warrant the latter's seeking the intervention of the Minister of Finance by way of protection against me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I did not say that.

I took issue with the governor of the Bank of Canada; I took serious issue. However, I tell my hon. friend that I took my issue with him in an open manner. I was not afraid to tell the governor of the Bank of Canada what I thought about the policies of the investment committee of the unemployment insurance commission. I therefore stand today with the Leader of the Opposition, not as a protagonist for all that the governor of the Bank of Canada has done. I believe in the desired stability of the Bank of Canada and because I believe in fair play and British justice, I say that the only way in which satisfactorily to conclude this matter is to give the governor of the Bank of Canada an opportunity to answer the Minister of Finance before a responsible committee of this house.
Here is another letter from the governor of the Bank of Canada dated June 26, in which he states this:
What is at issue here is the right of Canadians to know why I refused to meet the demand of the government.
If it is the right of Canadians to know this, it is also the right of their representatives in parliament; and that is why we want a committee. The governor goes on to state this:
The terms of Bill 114 make it clear that you, Mr. Fleming, and the government are still not prepared to accept a broad and ultimate responsibility for monetary policy, but merely want to have the power to change the governor at a time when it suits your political purposes to do so.
That is a serious charge. Is it true? That is a charge made by the governor. Let us confront him and find out whether that is the fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not true.

If it is not true, then let us determine that fact in a committee. On that committee will be a majority of members of the Conservative party. They can listen to this charge and they can determine, in their objective manner, whether or not it is true, that the government has acted only for political purposes.
Then the governor goes on to say this:
The point which I am concerned to bring before public opinion-and which you, Mr. Fleming, and the government are trying to prevent me from bringing before a parliamentary committee-is that the position of governor of Canada's central bank will be destroyed, and the whole institution will become merely an arm of a political machine, if the governor is to be terrorized into resigning whenever the government of the day wants him to, without any issue of policy being raised, without the government stating its monetary policy in parliament or elsewhere, and without the government accepting responsibility for monetary policy.
Governor of Bank of Canada
Those are serious charges. In the face of the bill of rights, in the face of the attack made by the Prime Minister on any violation of the rule of law, are we in this house going to take the position now, in the face of these serious charges, that this house must make its mind up on the mere say-so of a prejudiced Minister of Finance?
Then on page 3 of his letter of June 26 the governor goes on to state this-
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a question?

At the end of my
speech I shall be glad to answer any questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Essex East has the floor.

In his letter of June 26 the governor goes on to state this:
On March 20th after telling them of my talk with you, Mr. Fleming, (of March 18) I asked them in open meeting whether any of them felt I should resign. Every one of them said, "No".
I say to the Minister of Finance now that it was a result of his intervention that action was taken by the directors, not in accordance with the terms of section 5 of the Bank of Canada Act but in spite of those terms, that the directors expressed their regret in asking for the resignation of the governor of the Bank of Canada. I say that the Minister of Finance had no right to do that. I charge him now, first of all with improper relations with the directors of the bank.
Oh, oh.

I charge him with exercising unfair duress on the directors of the bank. Hon. gentlemen may laugh, but the people of Canada will not laugh when the facts of this matter are properly exposed. Then I ask hon. gentlemen to laugh at this. The governor goes on to point out at page 4:
You, Mr. Fleming, were told by Mr. Bryden about a possible change in these provisions six months before the directors acted in February, 1960 and you have a letter from Mr. Bryden to prove it, which you persist in concealing.
Oh, oh.

The governor goes on:
The deputy minister of finance was told by Mr. Bryden about the actual proposed action a week before the directors' meeting at which action was taken and he said he thought the proposed change was reasonable.
I would like to examine the governor on the matter of pension. I would like to examine the board of directors on all the circumstances of this pension. I am told that Mr. Bryden is a close friend of the Minister of Finance. I

Governor of Bank of Canada am told that he was a supporter of the Minister of Finance and a worker in the minister's electoral interests. I am told that Mr. Bryden, after taking the initiative in the meeting of the board of directors, discussed this matter within ten days of that meeting with the Minister of Finance-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.

-and yet the
Minister of Finance told us the other day that he did not know of this except in the month of February last.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.
Yes, you did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said I first heard of it in the spring of 1961.

I challenge the minister to deny that he was told by Mr. Bryden long before that, not only of the fact but the reasons which prompted him to take the initiative that he did take with regard to this pension about which, as one member of this house, I would like in turn to question the governor and the directors of the bank, to ascertain what are all the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the hon. member challenging my statement and saying that I heard about this action taken by the board on February 15, 1960-
I have made my statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -within ten days of that meeting, or some time before-
I say, within ten days.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say that statement is utterly false, Mr. Speaker. I repeat what I said earlier, that I first learned of the action taken by the board of directors on February 15, 1960 in the spring of 1961.
Where is your flag?

Let me read further what the governor said:
I believe the public are entitled to have these charges and the true facts reviewed by a parliamentary committee-before I am wrongfully removed from office-and to have all aspects of the matter brought out and considered. I demand that they be reviewed by a parliamentary committee where I can be given a fair opportunity to be heard, and where they can be submitted to the judgment of public opinion. The use of smear tactics, and the attempt to intimidate public servants with the idea that smear tactics will be used against them in public if they do not bow to improper suggestions from the government, should not be allowed to go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Here is where the smear lies; you are spreading it.
My hon. friend means the Bryden matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am referring to what you just read.

Let me read it again:
You, Mr. Fleming, were told by Mr. Bryden about a possible change in these provisions six months before the directors acted in February, 1960 and you have a letter from Mr. Bryden to prove it, which you persist in concealing.
There is the statement made by the governor. I am not saying it is true; I am not saying it is untrue; but I am saying it is not at all what the Minister of Finance said.
You are not saying anything at all.

It is contrary to what the Minister of Finance said, and we are entitled, surely, to ascertain in a matter of such fundamental importance which of the two witnesses, the Minister of Finance or the governor of the Bank of Canada, has made a statement in accordance with the facts. Are we now to be denied again, by one of the partisan witnesses, the Minister of Finance, the opportunity of contesting his statement or having a contrary view put forward by someone who does contest it? That is the issue, pure and simple.
This government has a large majority behind it. Hon. members opposite can pass this bill without any difficulty, if they want to. Tyranny of the majority is something that this government has exercised on other occasions before this particular one-
No, no.

-but that will not settle this matter in the minds of hon. members of this house or in the public mind, because whatever views there may exist in Canada at the present time regarding this regrettable matter, there is one view that one hears all over, and that is that the government has ineptly handled this whole situation and the only way to restore confidence is for the governor of the Bank of Canada to be given an opportunity of saying exactly what he believes the situation to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are saying it for him now.

In the final page of this letter we have this statement by the governor of the Bank of Canada. Here is the governor saying, "Give me my day in court. Put me under the provisions of the bill of rights. Let the rule of law apply to me. Let me not be denied justice. If you give me that

right, then I make this statement to you"- and here it is; and what more fair statement could one find? The governor writes:
If in the end, following such discussion, an honest difference of opinion proved to be unbridgeable, then it would be the duty of the governor to resign and to give the people of Canada a full explanation of the reasons for his resignation.
What could be more reasonable than that? Under the Bank of Canada Act the governor holds office for a period of seven years during good behaviour. The Minister of Finance has not alleged today that any of the circumstances which are put forward in an ex parte manner by him constitute a violation of the meaning of the phrase "good behaviour". Therefore the only way in which the governor can in law be compelled to resign is where there is a difference in policy; where first of all, let us say, in the field of monetary policy the government does not agree with the policy pursued by the governor of the bank.
That situation is not before us. The Minister of Finance says that is clearly not the situation, because under no circumstances does this government in any way accept responsibility for monetary policy, notwithstanding what may have been the position of preceding ministers of finance. Then in the field of public debt, in the field of financial policy, in fiscal matters, the governor has not up until very recently, we were told, expressed any views that embarrass the government or are not in accord with the government of today.
We learned there was disaccord only as a result of the revelations by the Minister of Finance this morning. It was only in the middle of May that there was a conflict in this regard. The minister need not look at me seriously as though he did not understand; he has repeatedly taken the position in this house that there was no dispute between the governor of the Bank of Canada and himself until a few days before we learned that he had asked for the resignation of the governor of the Bank of Canada, thereby-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is your imagination there.

-leaving open to public conjecture the inevitable suggestion that there were political reasons for the course the government took on May 30. It is significant that on May 29 four by-elections were held in this country and in those four byelections-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You got licked in three of them.

-the total vote was overwhelmingly against this government.
Governor of Bank of Canada The government had to look for a scapegoat, and what better scapegoat than the governor of the Bank of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We always had you.

That is the disgraceful position in which we have been placed. I say this to the Minister of Finance. For this kind of situation to have eventuated on the eve of the presentation of a budget represents, I suggest to him, a most irresponsible course of action. I am not alone in this thinking, because I find that the governor of the Bank of Canada says at page 2 of this letter:
In the absence of any other real explanation of the government's action it may yet be proved that political intentions were the real purpose of the move to get rid of me.
Is that true? Is that the true situation? Are we not to be given the opportunity of finding out whether there is any basis of fact for this statement which appears in today's letter of the governor of the Bank of Canada?
This matter has concerned the people of Canada. I am sure we are all aware of the public interest in this discussion. We have not had in many months as deep an interest in our affairs as we have had since the presentation of the budget in this situation known as the Coyne-Fleming affair. The result is, whether or not hon. gentlemen agree, all over the country there is disquietude. There is the feeling that this government, composed of men who have had no great business experience, have allowed themselves to get into a position where our financial structure stands in danger and where there is uncertainty whether it may be further endangered as a result of the dispute which has arisen between the head of the central bank and the government of this country. This has never happened before. This has never happened in any country where there is a central bank. It has never happened in the United States; it has never happened in the United Kingdom; it has never happened in any of the Scandinavian countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There is only one Coyne, that is why.
There is only one Fleming.

The reason this has happened in this country is that we have a government which is prepared to prostitute the interests of the nation in furthering its own political advancement. If that statement is found to be too strong, then the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) and the other ministers

Governor of Bank of Canada who are here have the opportunity to live up to the terms of the bill of rights which they have put on sheepskin, which they have distributed all over this country as a symbol of fundamental freedoms and liberties in Canada. Let us have as a first manifestation of the integrity of that expressed faith an acceptance of the proposal that in a matter of this importance where no protagonistic position is taken by the Liberal opposition, for or against, we should give to the accused an opportunity of stating his side of the case.
The Minister of Finance need not sit there in great smugness. He may be able to show that certain banking institutions and others in this country feel that this matter has, finally, to be resolved. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, undoubtedly this regrettable situation has reached the point where the usefulness of the governor has been impaired. But that position has been brought about by the way in which this matter has been handled by the government and in particular, I regret to say, by the Minister of Finance. I cannot believe that the Minister of Finance having taken the position throughout all these months that there was no disagreement between himself and the governor could have agreed in the dying days of the month of May to take the course he did without the greatest pressure being put on him by his colleagues and perhaps by the Prime Minister. We do know that we had been seeking for weeks to ascertain from the Minister of Finance when he was going to bring down his budget, a budget that had been delayed as no other budget in our history had been delayed. Undoubtedly, there were special reasons. We now perhaps have found what some of those circumstances are in the letter of June 26 circulated today by the governor of the Bank of Canada when apparently in the mind of the minister was a budget of an altogether different type from the one put forward the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a false statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

speakeroldname: Mr. Egan Chambers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It is always most interesting to listen to the hon. member for Essex East. I have found it fascinating from time to time to follow his grandiloquent rhetoric, his rolling inconsistencies, and I have often wondered where he picked up that particular style. I have wondered where, in the background, was his mentor. I came across it the other day in a book which gives an account of a speech by

the Hon. A. E. Windheaver some years ago. I should like to quote briefly from this speech in order to show the similarity of style:
Literary movements grow, fashions change, and people leave the country. But geology is founded upon a rock. The great Liberal party, which I have the honour to represent and which is not responsible for these roads, may some day pass away. But when that day comes, and I say it advisedly, when that day comes, the price of wheat will be down to 20 cents, f.o.b. Fort William, the fodder crops will rot in the fields, and these here roads will be the home of the rearing cactus and the gopher. The Liberal party has always fought against that type of thing. But when that day comes, I want to say that geology will still be geology. We've got the whole north country unexplored and undeveloped. Think of it! Over four million square miles of solid rock. And we are going to use that money to put the agriculture of Saskatchewan on a solid footing.
It is sometimes a useful trick.
May I call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 7.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker,-
All the young members of the Tory party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I trust the Hansard reporter caught that remark of the hon. member for Essex East, because it is exactly those young members of the Conservative party who are most concerned with the issue facing us tonight.
They should be concerned with human freedom.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The issue is one of responsible government. The question before this parliament today is how we should be governed, whether our policy should be made by those who have been elected by the people of Canada or by officials.
The young members of the Conservative party to whom the hon. member made reference take their stand quite squarely in favour of responsible government, in favour of having the conduct of our affairs in the hands of those who have been chosen by the people of Canada. Under our system, when any issue arises between those who have been elected and chosen by the people to conduct their affairs, and those who have been appointed as officials, then the elected government must prevail.
No doubt about that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We are really not concerned with what the policy differences are between the Minister of Finance and the Bank of Canada; what concerns us is the fact that the disagreement exists and, as has now been demonstrated by the public utterances of the governor, those differences are certainly on his side, irreconcilable. We have evidence now in the public press, in the frequent publicity hand-outs of the governor-
Twenty five pages.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
-of the type of difficulty that the Minister of Finance has been faced with over the last four years. The only comment I can make on that is one of amazement at the extraordinary patience of the Minister of Finance in the face of such an attitude.
This afternoon the hon. member for Essex East made much of the bill of rights. The bill of rights is a most important enactment. The right we are concerned with here is that of the people to be governed and to have their policies formulated by people of their own choice.
Let us consider for a moment what the Leader of the Opposition would do were he faced with a similar situation, and we have some evidence in that regard because at a press conference on television the other day he was asked a question and his reply was as follows:
It never need have arisen-
He was referring to the controversy. He went on:
-and when it did arise between the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada, surely that is where and when the Prime Minister of this country should have stepped in, taken his responsibility and settled this matter.
He was then asked this question:
And ask for Mr. Coyne's resignation?
This is his answer:
And settled this matter in a way which would not have resulted in public controversy and it could have been done, I am sure.
Today this same hon. gentleman rises in this house and says that this whole matter should be debated before a committee of the house. Here surely is a way to avoid public controversy; here surely is a way to maintain the integrity and dignity of the Bank of Canada, which are so important to our reputation both nationally and internationally. In effect, what the Leader of the Opposition has said is that the government should have tried to arrange for the governor of the Bank of Canada to go quietly. This is exactly what the Minister of Finance did, Mr. Speaker.
90205-6-447
Governor of Bank of Canada
Over the years the Minister of Finance withstood the embarrassment that was created for him by the public utterances of the governor.
For him, yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The minister defended him in the house. He has tried in every way to reach an understanding whereby the governor of the Bank of Canada would see his duty. When the time came that it became evident beyond all question that it was impossible to instruct the governor in his duties, he then tried to give the governor a way of gracefully withdrawing without any public controversy, as the Leader of the Opposition has recommended. The governor would then have had the choice of keeping his peace or as a citizen making whatever statements he felt should be made on the public platform because every citizen has that right except those whose duty it is to co-operate with the government in the fulfilling of the policies that the government lays down.
Instead of accepting the offer that the Minister of Finance made, what has happened? The governor embarked on an open attack on the Minister of Finance and the government. Using all the resources of political publicity, using all the resources of the bank, which were not designed for such a purpose, he attempted to muster public opinion behind his views and to cast discredit on the views of the Minister of Finance and the government.
Hon. members in the opposition say that the governor must be heard. Be heard. We have heard nothing else in the last few weeks. The noise of the governor is deafening. How has he been heard? He has been heard in a political attack on the government of the day on questions many of which are not in the realm of the responsibilities of the Bank of Canada. This is political action, Mr. Speaker, and I for one would welcome the governor of the bank on the political battlefield when he so arranges his affairs that he is eligible to take up that position. So far he has not. He even goes so far in his latest communique as to speak of elections.
Everyone in Canada has the right to discuss politics and elections but in the case of a public official he must first resign. This is the long tradition that has been observed in this country and in those other countries whose traditions we share. Many times a public servant has found himself in such disagreement with the government that he feels he can no longer carry on. The honourable course has been known for years. He must first resign and then make his views known. This was the course that the governor rejected.

Governor of Bank of Canada
It is suggested, according to the amendment, that we should place this whole matter before a committee of the house, and it is interesting, it seems to me, to speculate on why members of the opposition would like to follow this course. They would like to follow it because they want to see before that committee a debate on policy between the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada. They themselves have not the desire or the courages-or whatever it may be-to espouse the policies of the governor but they think the enuciation of these policies before a committee might damage the Minister of Finance, and that is what they want. The fact that it would also damage the Bank of Canada, damage our public credit at home and abroad, means nothing to them. Not at all. Let us have the circus. Never mind what happens to Canada's position in the world. Let us have the circus. Let us see if we can damage the Minister of Finance. This kind of thing would be unprecedented.
It has been forecast that there will be a royal commission that will investigate this whole area of our public affairs. It is not possible to forecast what witnesses such a commission would call but it is perfectly conceivable that the governor of the Bank of Canada, having resigned and having recaptured his right to public comment, could ask to appear before that commission. Our concern, Mr. Speaker, is to get over this unfortunate matter with the least damage to the Bank of Canada and to the credit of Canada as a whole.
The forum for debate of fiscal and monetary policies is here in this house and the people who are chosen by the electors of Canada to conduct that debate are here in this house. For our side they are the Minister of Finance, his colleagues and those who sit behind him, and for the side of the opposition similarly it is those who have been elected for that purpose. Here is where the debate should take place between those who represent varying degrees of opinion in the country, not in a debate between elected representatives and public officials.
I mentioned a few moments ago that the governor had taken a most extraordinary course. Instead of resigning, as tradition demanded, and then making his views known, instead of accepting the offer of the Minister of Finance to let him conform to our traditions with dignity and resign, he chose the one way that is forbidden to public officials. He chose political action. I must say that he has been a keen student of political action, and I wonder whether possibly some member who sits across the floor has found himself in a position to advise him on tactics.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It sounds like it.
Let us have a committee and find that out too.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No doubt as opportunity arises those hon. gentlemen who are friendly with the governor will be in a position to deny this. But certainly he showed great tactical skill in the release of the letters at a time when the minister was in the house and had no opportunity to prepare a reply, the release today of a letter dated June 26 which was delivered, I understand, to the office of the Minister of Finance over in the Confederation building when he was here, but somehow was also-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One hour after it was given to the press.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: One hour after it was given to the press, and not only here but somehow also at about the same time it was delivered to newspaper offices at least in Montreal and I suspect in the rest of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Through local Bank of Canada offices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I was able to get a copy of this letter by telephoning the public relations department of the Bank of Canada. They informed me that copies were available.
The minister had it just as fast as we had it in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I got it one hour after it was released to the press. Did you get that?
He is just copying the minister's technique.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There has been some question whether in fact a sufficient degree of disagreement existed between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the government that he should resign. There is another factor which, as far as I know, has not been considered. I refer to section 16 of the Bank of Canada Act which reads as follows:
Every director, officer, clerk and employee of the banks shall before entering upon his duties take before a justice of the peace or a commissioner for taking affidavits, an oath of fidelity and secrecy in the form prescribed in schedule A.
The first part of schedule A can be summarized by saying that it is the oath to faithfully fulfil the duties, but the second part I should like to quote as follows:
I further solemnly swear that I will not communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled thereto any information relating to the affairs of the bank, nor will I allow any such person to inspect or have access to any

books or documents belonging to or in the possession of the bank and relating to the business of the bank.
Mr. Speaker, apart from whatever else may be said, it is my contention that the governor of the Bank of Canada is in violation of that oath. Such being the case, this is not the time for prolonging a controversy, as the Leader of the Opposition has suggested, and I agree with him. This is not the time for dragging out things which will do further damage to the bank and the country. This governor should stand not upon the order of his going, but go at once.
Mr. Speaker, will the hon. member permit a question?
No.
I am directing a question to you.
Oh, 1 beg your pardon.

I should like to ask the hon. member whether or not the very voluminous documents that have come from Mr. Coyne's office, not only to us but to all parts of Canada, have been paid for by himself or by the government of Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I cannot go any further than to say the documents I have obtained today were obtained from the public relations department of the Bank of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, there was one observation made by my friend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) with which I profoundly agree and which goes to the very basis of this debate today. My hon. friend said that there could not be two sovereignties in this country. He was absolutely right. It is perfectly obvious, sir, that-
Heads will roll.

It is perfectly obvious, sir, that there is only one sovereignty in this country and that is this parliament. There has not been one jot or tittle of evidence produced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) or by either of the two hon. gentlemen who have spoken for him to suggest that the governor of the Bank of Canada in anything that he did at any time sought to usurp the power of the government.
Where have you been, Jack?

I have paid as much attention to this matter as anyone has. There is abundant evidence that this government, which is the servant of this house, has usurped the rights of parliament. The minister beat his breast over and over again disclaiming 90205-6-4474
Governor of Bank of Canada the responsibility which was his and which Mr. Coyne has urged him to assume.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, he did not.

As my friend the hon. member for Essex East pointed out this afternoon, the minister has dodged and shirked his responsibility and when he got in a jam he got orders from the east block-from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)-to get rid of Coyne. The minister then went behind the back of this parliament-he sneaked behind the back of this parliament-in an attempt to get the governor to leave, as he says, with dignity and as quietly as possible.
The minister himself has told us that the governor was responsible to parliament, not to the government, yet the minister seeks to undermine parliament by taking away the rights of parliament, assuming them for himself, in seeking to make a secret deal, conniving to make a deal with Mr. Coyne about which, if Mr. Coyne had complied, this parliament would never have known of. That is the kind of thing that has been happening. If Mr. Coyne had been as gutless as the Minister of Finance showed himself to be by his speech this afternoon when he talked about not having had the courage to take this step for four years, he might have succeeded and Mr. Coyne would then have supinely gone his way. He did not because, whatever else you can say about Mr. Coyne, you cannot say that he has not got courage.
He certainly has got gall.

No one can say that he has not got a high sense of his responsibility to this parliament. I say that the Minister of Finance confessed the other day that he tried to usurp the rights of parliament by putting himself in the place of parliament. That is what he tried to do. This is all the more extraordinary when one recalls some of the things that have been said by the Minister of Finance in the past. I intend to recall only one of them, because it is very relevant. The Minister of Finance in 1955-
Mr. Speaker, I should like to rise on a question of privilege.
In 1955 the Minister of Finance-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Stormont is rising on a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has endeavoured to mislead the house in that he said there was not one jot or tittle of evidence that Mr. Coyne endeavoured to usurp the prerogatives of this

Governor of Bank of Canada house. I contend that he has usurped the prerogatives of this house because, as the Leader of the Opposition stated-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, order. Will the hon. member please resume his seat. The hon. member, as he has indicated himself, is presenting a contention, not raising a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, I was about to recall to this house, and perhaps to the hon. members who have been more recently elected, one of many statements in respect to the rights of parliament made by the present Minister of Finance in the year 1955 when that hon. member professed to have some concern for the rights of parliament, which he has certainly not demonstrated since the day he took his seat on the treasury benches. Not even excepting his leader, no other member on the treasury benches has shown uniformly the contempt for parliament and for the members of parliament, or for the opposition, that the hon. gentleman has shown throughout his term there. In those days when he was over here showing contempt for the Speaker and the Chair, which was his main line when he was over here-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is more foolishness.
Well, you just don't like it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is just more foolishness.

You do not want to hear what the minister said as a private member, but I think it ought to be on the record. The minister quoted these words:
"Parliament is the grand inquest which has the right to inquire into anything and everything."
Those were the words of a man who spent a great deal of his life holding ministerial power in Canada; those were words uttered in 1861 by Sir John A. Macdonald. In those days parliament was a grand inquest with the right to inquire into everything and anything, but it is not today, when we see secrecy imposed by the government, and hon. members of this house in the discharge of their solemn obligations to the constituents who elected them denied information they ought to have.
If ever any minister was convicted out of his own mouth, the minister convicts himself in respect to this bill by those words which he uttered in this house some years ago, because he denied on a pretext of secrecy the answers to questions asked by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan). He denied Mr. Bryden's letter in getting these-well, sir, I will not go into that. We have not got Mr. Bryden's letter but we now know what was contained in it and why it was denied to this house.
His leader, the Prime Minister, had the effrontery, on the very day he asked his


followers to vote to suppress that information here in this house, to go on the air and say that the case of the governor of the Bank of Canada was now out in the open where it could be thoroughly discussed and assessed in the light of the facts. That is what the Prime Minister told the people of Canada on television. That statement is patently false. The Prime Minister made it false that very day in this house by denying the information to us. He has joined or indeed led his government into suppressing this information which parliament is entitled to have if it is the grand inquest the minister said it was and which it ought to be. This is the most extraordinary procedure. Of course, it is characteristic of that careless use of language found in every reference the Prime Minister made to Mr. Coyne, including describing him as a civil servant. If the Prime Minister does not know better, he ought to do so. If he does know better, he was trying to mislead the people. Hon. gentlemen can have it either way. It does not seem to me to make much difference which view you take of it, it is not very creditable to the Prime Minister of this country. Nor is it very creditable to the Prime Minister of this country who allowed, according to the Minister of Finance, this situation to persist for four years while doing nothing about it, and who apparently made not the slightest effort to compose this difference, and who then seeks to exacerbate it by going on the air and making statements that are not in accord with the facts which were established in this house on the very same day.
As hon. members know, I have had some association in the past with real prime ministers who attended to the administration of the country and did not merely conduct a constant political campaign. We have had a continuous election campaign in this country since the spring of 1957, and the Prime Minister has never had time, in the midst of this election campaign, to give any attention to the government of this country. That is one of the principal reasons this country is in the shocking mess it is in.
Oh, oh.

When hon. gentlemen
realized that in 1961 the public at last had twigged to the fact that they were responsible for the mess, after they had blamed the Liberals in 1958, they had blamed the Americans in 1959, and then in 1960 they had a recovery; and we know what happened to that recovery. We remember the minister's boast about a balanced budget and the unemployment going with the snow. That is a fair indication of the kind of leadership we have had from this

minister. When he found himself so hopelessly wrong in 1961 he says, "I have got to have a victim; I have got to take attention away from myself". Maybe he said it or maybe it was the Prime Minister who ordered him to do it. I suspect the latter. It is an extraordinary thing, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out earlier today, that there seems to have been an amazing consonance of view, not dissonance, between the governor of the bank and the Minister of Finance right up to a date as late as the minister's speech in January, 1961, in Brantford and which the governor might equally well have made. This sudden conversion, this turning of Saul into Paul that happened some time in the spring,-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no.

-this great light that suddenly came upon this former pagan, this conversion to expansion, the expansion that only a few months ago he was decrying, was worrying about, as I say, was an extraordinary change indeed. But, oh, no; the governor must go and he must go quietly in order to preserve the dignity of the Bank of Canada and to conceal the facts from the people of Canada and the parliament of Canada. What instrument do they use to do it when the governor refuses to resign? Do they come here in parliament and make their case? Do they allow us to perform our functions as an opposition? Do they allow this parliament to be sovereign? No, Mr. Speaker. They say, "We have a huge and servile majority; we will put a bill through this house to take away the rights of this man without letting him be heard".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Nonsense.
That is what you are doing. It is precisely what you are doing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He is in the headlines every day.

As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Carleton who, I believe, is a member of the bar, is now suggesting to us that if a man makes a statement in public outside the courts, he is to be denied his right to access to the courts. If that is the new doctrine of the bill of rights, it is not a doctrine that any Liberal could espouse, but it is perhaps what one would expect from the hon. gentleman opposite.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman indicate to the house whether he has been in communication with Mr. Coyne since the first of June?
Governor of Bank of Canada
Oh, oh.
I am making a speech. I realize, of course, how effective the interruption will be.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman allowed me to ask the question; apparently he does not wish to answer it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If there is an answer, I would be unable to hear it.

It is a very well known fact that I have known Mr. Coyne for 30 years and that he is one of my personal friends. I live in a free country and of course I have not denied myself communication with my friends, even under this Tory despotism.
Oh, oh.
If hon. gentlemen maintain a gestapo so far as public servants are concerned in this country, they can boast about it in this company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The bubble is pricked now; now we know.
Any member of parliament can phone him. I have not done so, but I have known him equally long.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I am going to say something I had not intended to say in this house. It is also known, I think, to a few hon. members that I had a brother who was beaten to death by the nazis in a concentration camp at Buchenwald; and no one will ever make me vote for legislation to condemn a man without a hearing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Why did you not say that when you threw Bob Pitt out of a job without a hearing? I refer to Bob Pitt of Winnipeg and Saskatoon. What hypocrisy it is to make such a statement now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Saskatoon forgets that the floor is now held by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate. Those who wish to speak will have an opportunity of doing so only if they allow one member to continue at a time.

I said that this was a bill of attainder. I said that this was a procedure which was now unknown to our practice, and which is forbidden by the constitution of the United States, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out this afternoon. I should like to read to you, Mr. Speaker, because it is so apt, the description of a bill of attainder found in the encyclopedia Britannica, the

Governor of Bank of Canada 1959 edition. I hope hon. members opposite will listen very carefully to the language of it. It is as follows:
First passed in 1459, such bills were employed, more particularly during the reigns of the Tudor kings, as a species of extrajudicial procedure, for the direct punishment of political offences. Dispensing with the ordinary judicial forms and precedents, they took away from the accused whatever advantages he might have gained in the courts of law; such evidence only was admitted as might be necessary to secure conviction; indeed, in many cases bills of attainder were passed without any evidence being produced at all.
As is the case here.
In the reign of Henry VIII they were much used, through a subservient parliament, to punish those who had incurred the king's displeasure; many distinguished victims who could not have been charged with any offence under the existing laws being by this means disposed of.
That, sir, is very simply what the government is asking us to do in this case.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Rot.

That is the reason why the Leader of the Opposition made the amendment he did to provide an opportunity to Mr. Coyne, who needs no defence from anyone else, who is perfectly capable of defending himself if this parliament will allow him to do so. If there is enough freedom left in this house to allow him to do so, if there is enough sense of justice in this house left to allow him to do so, he will need no defence from any of us nor should he get any. He should be allowed to defend himself and to explain himself. Why? Because he is one of that very limited group of persons who, under the statutes of this parliament, apart from the judges, are appointed during good behaviour. What does that historic phrase mean? It seems that many hon. gentlemen opposite have lost the sense of it. It means the government, the executive, must not in any way seek to remove those people except by showing cause, and doing so openly in this parliament, not secretly behind closed doors. That is what it means.
What the minister did on May 30 in his office was done behind closed doors, when he asked Mr. Coyne to go quietly so that his family would not suffer and so that the dignity of his office would not suffer, and so the government would not be embarrassed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I said nothing about the family at any time. That is a red herring that has been brought into this matter by the hon. member. Never was a word said about the family.

Well, it was certainly behind closed doors; it was certainly done in secret and parliament was not intended to


know anything about it except the fact that Mr. Coyne had quietly resigned and gone away, so parliament would never know what design the government had after they got rid of him.
As my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition pointed out this morning, it is exactly equivalent to asking us to pass a bill to remove the chairman of the civil service commission because, say, the Minister of Finance does not like the colour of his eyes, to put someone else there who will give the jobs to the hon. gentleman's friends. That is exactly the same thing.
Oh, oh.
Of course it is.
Nonsense.

The chairman of the civil service commission is appointed during good behaviour. It is fortunate that statute contains an additional provision that there must be an address of both houses. The Bank of Canada Act does not, but there is no doubt the intention was the same in both. The same is true about the president of the C.B.C. This government tried to have him appointed during pleasure and we did our best to have an amendment passed in this house to include good behaviour. Our amendment was refused.
However, hon. ladies and gentlemen in the other place, having more respect than was shown by the majority here for the rights of the people and for the non-partisan character that the broadcasting service must necessarily have, amended that legislation. This government reluctantly accepted that amendment in 1958 in order to give a measure of independence of partisan control to broadcasting.
Parliament decided that civil servants should be above partisan control, and parliament decided that the electoral system should be above partisan control, and parliament decided that the Auditor General should be above partisan control. There is no difference between this bill and bringing in a bill to remove the Auditor General and declare his office vacant without any cause given. Perhaps if that were done hon. gentlemen could appoint someone who would not look into the hospital grants, for example, and who would be more complacent with regard to some of the activities that some hon. gentlemen opposite seem to find so interesting in these times.
I say that the provision that these offices that parliament said were to be held during good behaviour, whose incumbents were to be removed only for cause, cause shown in open assembly and in open court and with the right of discussion, was made for a reason.

That was done to prevent what the Prime Minister spoke about on June 4, 1955, in the days when the Prime Minister was still interested in these things; those days seem to have vanished:
... there has been no suggestion on the part of the government that it intends to deviate one whit from the trend that apparently is to be followed, of establishing for ministers of the crown and this government an absolutism.
That is what they are seeking to do by this bill so tar as the Bank of Canada is concerned. If they can get rid of Mr. Coyne without giving any reasons; if they can use the tyranny of a majority to clear him out, to get that block out of the way, as the Prime Minister so felicitously put it-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: When did the majority become a tyranny? Is that a new thesis in this country?

I commend to the hon. gentleman the pipe line debate. He seems to have forgotten that we heard a lot about the rights of the minority from some hon. gentlemen opposite in those days. That has all been forgotten now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all: you are still speaking, we were not allowed to speak then.

They have not quite dared to expel the opposition from this house. This is a man that a previous parliament decided could only be removed by cause, whom they do not allow to say a word in his own defence in the only place where he could be cross-examined. This is just one more step in that direction.
Why did previous parliaments decide that the governor and the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada should be appointed during good behaviour and should be removable only for cause? The answer is very obvious. It was given by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon. It is because in no free country, with a constitutional government, would a partisan executive be given the uncontrolled right to start the printing presses. The most ancient of all our rights is the right of the elected representatives of the people to decide what the taxes will be. There is no taxation that is so unfair, so insidious or so inexorable as inflation and there is no doubt whatsoever that this block that Mr. Coyne was, according to the Prime Minister, was a block to that uncontrolled right. First they got a collection of Tory hacks as members of the board of directors. They did not dare to act against Mr. Coyne-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Shame on you.
I am not a bit ashamed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You should be.
Governor of Bank of Canada
One of them was a defeated Tory candidate and has been running around here ever since.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is what the hon. gentleman will be after the next election.

They had to get them first, and they had to wait for four years. After waiting four years, these men yielded to the crack of the minister's whip and did what they were told to do; they passed the resolution he dictated to them-
Improperly.
improperly-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is untrue.
that was dictated by the Minister of Finance behind the back of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is utterly untrue. That is a false statement.
Of course, you will not let us go to a committee where we can find out whether or not it is true.
You are the accused now.
Let us see these directors and ask them questions.
Hear, hear.
The only person who has any voice in this parliament is the accuser.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Keep them out of Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You could telephone one of them. You telephoned Mr. Coyne.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Telephone Jim again.

What is this alleged dispute about? What is this supposed adequate reason on the minister's say-so, without any evidence, without any supporting documents, without any chance for us, the representatives of the people, the sovereign people, to examine Mr. Coyne or to examine the directors? We have to take the word of this omnipotent little minister, this omnipotent little creature of parliament who sets himself up above parliament and says, "You must do what we say". If they get away with this-
Mr. Pallet!: The hon. member sounds like eviscerated poultry right now.

If they get away with this in the case of Mr. Coyne, it does not matter who they appoint; it does not matter how eminent he is; the new governor is going to know they have done it once-and that, of course, is the way of dictators; you do it once and then it is a lot easier to do it the next time-and he is going to hesitate a long time before he fails to do whatever he is

Governor of Bank of Canada ordered to do by the Minister of Finance or the successor of the Minister of Finance.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, as I said the other evening, that the Minister of Finance himself is not going to survive this debate very long. He has made a mess of this business and the Prime Minister will not forget it.
We will see.
I say-
If he does not resign, he will be fired.
