I say that the fundamental reason why this matter is so important is not Mr. Coyne at all; it is the office of governor; it is the necessary independence in that office to protect the value of our money. I predict that if this government gets away with this measure; if they can appoint their stooge as governor-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Shame on you.
-that within six months the Canadian dollar will look like that, and in a year it will look like that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a mischievous, false statement.

What these ministers are confronted with is an impossible deficit. They have not got the courage to deal with it in a proper fashion and they want some subservient person in that office to start the printing presses. That is what they want. That is the real danger to the people of this country. That is why parliament provided that the governor could only be removed for cause given in open court, and that is why it is the duty of the governor even if he has only a suspicion of the motives of the government, to do what Mr. Coyne has done.
I would like to quote in this connection some of the evidence given by Mr. Graham Towers before the committee on banking and commerce in 1954 as reported in the proceedings of the committee for that year. I think it was on March 16. This is very relevant to what we are discussing, and nothing could be more important to the people, than this question of the money supply in this country and effective parliamentary control over it. Mr. Towers said:
The situation is that parliament has placed squarely on the shoulders of the directors and management of the Bank of Canada the responsibility for monetary policy. It would be of no use for us to come before a committee of this kind and say in respect to certain actions which were criticized, we did not like that, but the government wanted us to do it. The proper question would be: in what act has parliament said that you should do something in the field of monetary policy in which you do not believe? Therefore, we must and do take full responsibility for everything which we have done. Now, I think myself that the 
Bank of Canada Act is in this respect a very good act, and better than most, because it is clear. There is no alibi possible for the central bank.
This is the really important part, and it is something the minister does not seem ever to have understood:
On the other hand, there is no alibi possible for the government, because if government said: well, we disagreed with what the central bank did, but parliament has placed the responsibility on them, so what could we do? The answer obviously is that the administration of the day, supported by a majority in parliament, can always alter the legislation.
But not decapitate the governor-alter the legislation. Mr. Towers went on to say:
In fact, I doubt whether a disagreement would ever necessitate such a thing, because there are various ways and means by which directors and management can be got rid of.
Mr. Towers spoke, perhaps, better than he knew.
I am sure that in the case of a serious disagreement that is what would take place. There is a long history behind this thing in central banking- and I assure you I won't take up much more of the committee's time-but in the days when kings and princes ruled the roost, they had rather a nasty habit of debasing the coinage when they got into a fix, and even later on parliamentary governments sometimes did the same thing, in the modern sense of inflation. Therefore, it is interesting to notice that in all the many countries of the world-I think it is 60 or more which have central banks-they have always been set up not as a department of government but as separate institutions. In many cases, they have been nationalized, but they have been left as separate structures with the idea that then there are certain checks in respect to the possibility of doing that insidious thing which not one person in a million understands, debasing the currency. In some cases, of course, the independence, while intended to be encouraging to the public, is a pure fagade. Obviously that is so in a totalitarian state. But even in some other places in recent years there have been governments-we have had them in sister countries of the commonwealth-which felt that they could not bear the thought that even for a day someone should frustrate or delay the policy of the administration of the day. So on top of the fagade which, so far as the public is concerned was supposed to convey an idea of check and balance and independence, they would write in a clause saying the policy of the central bank shall be that dictated by the Minister of Finance from time to time. Myself, I think that that is a sort of mongrel arrangement, and the central bank should be either a pure department of government and known to the public as such, or it should have independent responsibility.
I am not sure Mr. Towers would say that today. We do know that Mr. Coyne does not say that. We do know that Mr. Coyne says the Bank of Canada should be in the same position as the Bank of England; that the Minister of Finance may in writing impose the views of the government, and if he does that and the governor disagrees and they cannot reconcile their differences, then the governor should resign. That is what Mr. Coyne has said. That is right. That is proper.

Governor of Bank of Canada But Mr. Coyne should not resign, and no governor should be expected to resign, merely because the minister does not like the colour of his hair or the amount of his pension or even some speech he has made. If Mr. Coyne had persisted in making speeches after the minister had said he should not make them that would have been another matter. The minister would have had a real cause and he could have come into the house and made his case, but he never protested at all. Instead, he came here and beat his breast and talked about freedom of speech and asked: would you deny freedom of speech to the governor of the Bank of Canada? That is what he said very recently. I could look it up if I had a little more time; it is familiar to all of us.
The plain fact of the matter is that there has not been the slightest evidence produced that the governor of the Bank of Canada by any act, as opposed, perhaps, to some words which the minister did not like, has been in conflict with the present administration. The minister may not have liked some of those words because they were embarrassing to the government inasmuch as they indicated that the government should be doing certain things which they were not doing. Apart from that, there is nothing, except for some mysterious thing in 1957. Either that incident in 1957 was important or it was not. If it was important, an issue should have been made of it then in parliament and Mr. Coyne should have been removed then. If it was not, does anybody in parliament, knowing the Minister of Finance as we all know him, think that if there was any incident more recent than that of 1957 he would have had to go back to 1957?
The plain fact is that any policy the bank has been asked to carry out, it has carried out. We know that, because we know that otherwise we would have heard a howl from the minister long ago. That is why the hon. gentleman would not answer the questions of my hon. friend from Welland. It is because he would have had to say "no" to both of those questions, and his whole case for the dismissal of the governor would have fallen completely to the ground if he had given a truthful answer to those questions. That is why the minister hid behind a pretence of secrecy.
As to this business of secrecy, it is perfectly true that in the ordinary operation there should be secrecy. The governor of the bank respected that to the letter until the minister fired him, or tried to. He then felt he had a duty to this parliament and to the people of Canada whose servant he was-not the servant of the government, not the servant of 90205-6-448
the minister, but the servant of parliament and the people of Canada. He felt it was his duty whatever happened to him to tell us that something was wrong and to give us a chance to find out. That is the issue. If there is something wrong with the governor, surely the government would be delighted to produce the evidence, delighted to give him a hearing and show he is wrong. Why is the government so scared? Why is the government so frightened?
Why do they not want this inquiry? The fact of the matter is that there is nothing substantial to inquire into. As a matter of fact they want a scapegoat for the past and-what I suspect is a great deal more serious-they want a compliant tool in the office of the governor of the Bank of Canada to deal with their deficits for the future.
Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public
Works): First, I wish to express the views of most of the members of this house in offering heartfelt congratulations to the Minister of Finance for the magnificent manner in which he has handled this whole Coyne affair. How he could have exercised the patience he has displayed, how he has had the wisdom that he has displayed, how he could have kept his dignity and decorum in the face of such constant insults and slights over a long period is beyond the understanding of most of the members of this house. Certainly he is a long suffering man and a man of very great mercy. If sympathy and kindness did not dominate his nature we could not have had a situation where a person who had become almost an anarchist would have been treated with such sympathy and understanding.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is tonight in a semi-hysterical state of mind, and I do not blame him for that. He has been under great strain and stress. We did not realize it; for not only is he conducting the business of the house, taking the place in parliament of the Leader of the Opposition, but at the same time he has been the confidential adviser of the governor of the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have a question of privilege here. I would simply say that that libel answers itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has admitted that he has been in constant touch with the governor, Mr. Speaker. I ask him to deny it; if he has not been in touch with the governor of the Bank of Canada. I will withdraw my remarks if he has not. Has he, or has he not?

I said I had been in touch with him as a friend.

Governor of Bank of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Well, out of his own mouth-

Perhaps the hon. gentleman would at least allow me to finish. I said I had been in touch with him as a friend of many, many years. I saw no reason, simply because of this action, to alter that friendship in any way whatsoever, nor do I think it is necessary to do so in a free country.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May I ask another question of the hon. member, since he is so willing to rise and answer these questions. These letters, reams of which I have been reading today, have a strange familiarity. I ask the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate this question. Did he not assist the governor of the Bank of Canada in the drafting of them, including the one of today?
The answer to that question is no.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The answer is no; all right, I have to accept the hon. member's answer in that regard.
The fact is that on the admission of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate we have a governor who has been aloof from political turmoil and the member for Bonavista-Twillingate has been in touch with him. I can only assume that the governor of the Bank of Canada has been accepting the advice of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Order. Shame.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I think it is a shame also; it is a crying shame that all these actions are not the actions of the person who we thought was a quiet, dignified banker but are the actions of the semi-hysterical member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Therefore, for the first time in this whole debate I have a certain sympathy for the governor of the bank who no doubt has been tremendously misguided.
May I ask this question. Is it not a fact that over the week end Her Majesty's loyal opposition have been in touch with the governor of the Bank of Canada-
Shame.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: -in an effort to have him resign now so that they will not have to vote on second reading of this bill? Is it not a fact that as late as last night the governor of the bank refused to resign?
I never knew how low one could sink.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Just a moment; out of the mouth of babes and sucklings, and the hon. member for-
I have been here longer than the minister and I will be here longer as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The hon. member has almost reached the summit of his career here and it will soon be over. When the vote is called -and I undersand the opposition is going to keep up this interminable delay for four days -I suggest that the official opposition to a man and to a woman will vote in favour of the governor of the Bank of Canada being discharged. There is no doubt about it; I challenge them to deny it.
We have a suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition today, the only one of which I have to take cognizance, that the governor of the Bank of Canada should have another "go" at this thing in a parliamentary committee. Here is a man who has explained his position in reams of well-written letters in the Pickersgillian style. Here is a man who has called press conferences at midnight, at any other hour of the day or night, either in Quebec or Ottawa, under some expert political coaching. He has given fabulous interviews. Here is a man who, as time creeps inevitably onward to bring to an end his meteoric career, kicks out in all directions. Here is a man who has appeared before a Senate committee to be cross-examined by members of the other place who have no interest in being re-elected, to be cross-examined by members of the political faith of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. After cross-examining him on all the speeches he has made up and down the country for a couple of years, what did they discover? They found out that he has no solution, no panacea, no facts, nothing to settle the problems which he himself has brought on. And yet, after that Senate committee hearing, it is now suggested by the Leader of the Opposition that this man, who is acting more like an anarchist than a governor of a bank, should be called before a committee of the House of Commons. Would I not like to have the opportunity of acting as counsel in that committee, of cross-examining him.
But why exacerbate the self-inflicted wounds of that poor man? I feel sorry for him for the first time because I know he has been misguided. But to bring him before a parliamentary committee at this time would be to create greater shame and greater degradation than have already taken place. And to what avail? What is there that can be brought out that was not brought out in the Senate committee? What is there that can be brought out now that we have the confidential letters which were put in the hands of the press before they reached parliament? What is there that can be said in this whole shameful story that has not been said already over and over again?
I think it is to the eternal credit of the Minister of Finance, who could have really

seen himself vindicated in a superlative degree by having this man appear before a parliamentary committee, that he has not seen fit to agree that this be done. Under all the circumstances it is a great pity that a man who held the rank of the governor of the Bank of Canada, whom we liked as a person and as a personality, should have been so badly advised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and others that he has set himself up on Mount Olympus superior to the government of Canada, and because this government represents an overwhelming majority of the people of Canada, in conflict with the people of Canada themselves.
I am not going to say very much about the increase in the pension from $12,000 to $25,000. Whether the increase was negotiated with the advice of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I do not know. But I can say this. From the time the governor of the Bank of Canada believed that even though he retired at the end of his term in December of this year he could feel secure with a pension of $25,000 a year with the hope of living another 30 years at a cost to the taxpayers of this country of three quarters of a million dollars, it is a fact, whether or not he was advised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in this connection, that from the time he got that increased pension he became bolder and bolder and bolder. He took issue from the Atlantic to the Pacific with whatever the government of Canada was doing, whether it was in the domain of banking or whether it was not. He invited, he urged that he should be fired. He urged that a year ago by his statements, and if I had been the minister of finance-and it is a good thing I was not-he would have been fired long ago and not on such terms as have happened under all the circumstances.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I say to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, whom I like personally but who is overwrought, distracted and somewhat hysterical, that when he comes back to his normal thinking ways after the summer holidays he will be very much ashamed of the scene he made in the house tonight. He will be terribly ashamed. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) at least had a reasoned speech but the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has just dealt in emotional pleas and in almost personal, bitter and degrading attacks on the Minister of Finance. I say to you, why do you keep saying that this is a little man? Why do you say that one of the greatest of Canada's finance ministers is little?
90205-6-4484
Governor of Bank of Canada
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I have heard this said over and over again and I think they must be referring to his physical size.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I call the minister's attention to the fact that it is customary to address the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: That is quite so. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I think we should continue to do that. Let us have an end of this whole thing. Let us get over this unfortunate incident which we all regret, which has now reached the realm of personalities and, believe me, I am not immune to that sort of thing. I admit that, but let us be done with it all. Let us bring down the curtain on this sad and unfortunate incident.
You would certainly like to.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The only explanation I can give is that this man, who has descended from the heights of Olympus to get into a political brawl and has conducted himself not like the gentleman I always thought he was, has now almost reached the stage of being an anarchist in his latest letter. I say, let us pity him. Surely, that speaks for itself. What did Mr. Abbott say? Mr. Abbott said, during the time he held office from 1946 to 1954:
The ultimate responsibility must fall upon the government.
By the way, that statement was quoted with approval by the present Leader of the Opposition.
Then we had a change, and this change is revealed in a statement made by Mr. Walter Harris who was finance minister from 1954 to 1957:
This action is the action of the governor of the bank and his responsibility alone.
When Harris made that statement, as set out in the Financial Post, may I suggest that that statement was understood only by the present governor of the Bank of Canada, because this action is the action of the governor of the bank and his responsibility alone. It was then that we got the tight money policy in Canada. I think that was one of the main issues in the past elections. I have heard many people talk about various issues, but one of the main issues was the tight money policy of the former government.
I shall say this in conclusion: I repeat, I do not know a time when there has been more unity in the party on any matter which has been brought into this house since I was elected in 1958. The backbenchers are behind the Minister of Finance. They have confidence in him. They know that if he is going to implement the kind of policy set out in the budget brought down by the government in June it can only be implemented if Coyne goes. I believe that the debate the Liberals are now carrying on-I do not know much about eastern Canada, but I know western Canada-is going to put them in this position. If they had any votes left before the debate started this morning they will have few left tomorrow morning if they keep on supporting Coyne and his tight money policy.

I wonder whether the hon. member for Bow River would permit a question?
Governor of Bank of Canada
Certainly.

In his speech, which I think missed the main point of debate, the hon. member stated that he had the privilege of appearing in all the courts of the land, including the highest court, which is of course this parliament. Can the hon. member tell the house whether he has ever pleaded in any court of the land where the accused was not present and indeed was not allowed to appear in his own defence, as is the case in this instance?

Mr. Speaker, my answer to that is exactly what I quoted from the Leader of the Opposition. Where there is a difference the governor must go. There is plenty of evidence, in fact there is reams of mail and that mail, those statements, in a criminal court, if they are used, can become evidence under certain circumstances. There is no rule governing that here. We have the evidence. All we need say to the Liberals is there is a difference, a difference between the policy of the governor of the Bank of Canada and the government. If anyone in the Liberal ranks can stand up now and say there is not a difference I wish to see that person stand in his place.

Mr. Speaker, if there was any doubt in our minds about the importance of this debate I think it has been dispelled by the fact that the government in its desperation to bull this thing through at any cost has called on its two best known hatchet men within the ranks. I am referring, of course, to the Minister of Public Works and the hon. member for Bow River. Both of these gentlemen have built up quite a reputation in the courts of this country as being outstanding lawyers. But I must say, Mr. Speaker, that if their performance across the country is as weak as it was tonight I wonder where they built up the reputation.
First of all, we had the Minister of Public Works who assumed that Mr. Coyne has been operating solely on the advice of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Well, I would say this is completely in keeping with the whole government case, because it is an assumption from first to last.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate listed some of the alibis that this government has used in the four years that it has been in office. Of course, he did not realize that his list would be out of date almost by the time he completed it. In 1958, the situation was all the fault of the Liberals. In 1959 it was the Americans; and in 1960 prosperity was around the corner. In 1961 it is Coyne and

Governor of Bank of Canada now, according to the Minister of Public Works, they even blame the Coyne affair on Pickersgill.
As far as the hon. member for Bow River is concerned, he first of all proceeded to establish the fact that this is the highest court in the land. There can be no question that he believes it is the highest court in the land. He referred to it many times. Then before this highest court whom or what did he call? He called a statement, a statement of the Leader of the Opposition. Well, unfortunately, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres this highest court in the land must operate on a statement and under no condition can we have witnesses appear before it. I also should like to know what other court in the land operates on this principle?
I personally would prefer to endorse the analysis of this problem as expounded by the Leader of the Opposition. I believe he put his finger right on the problem, which is, can any man in this country, let alone a key public servant, be condemned without a proper hearing?
Much to the surprise, and obviously much to the chagrin of the present government and in particular the Minister of Finance, Coyne did not do as he was supposed to do. He did not fold his tent and steal away in the middle of the night like an Arab. He was a man with enough courage to fight back.
One noticeable thing about the statements issued by Mr. Coyne is that they have been consistent throughout. He has never changed his story; it is the same today as it was when this case first broke.
I recall that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence said he was quite surprised at the tactics, the timing and so on of the statements that we read in our newspapers. It should be no surprise to the parliamentary secretary or to any other hon. member because Mr. Coyne was a very high officer working for a government which has governed by headlines in the last four years and he should be quite adept at headlines by this time.
There is one thing that we should emphasize, and it should be emphasized throughout this debate, namely that the governor of the Bank of Canada is almost within six months,
I believe, of completing his seven years which is the full term of his appointment. Four of those seven years have been served under this present government.
In contrast with the consistency of the arguments put forward by the governor of the Bank of Canada there has been complete and utter confusion on the part of the government, the Minister of Finance and other 

spokesmen of the government throughout this debate. They complained about the governor going to the press. At the time they complained about him they refused to allow him to appear before parliament to which he is responsible. No matter what efforts the opposition has made over the last four years to call the governor of the Bank of Canada before a parliamentary committee the request has always been refused by the government. If they will not permit the governor of the Bank of Canada to appear before parliament to which he is responsible what objection can they take to this gentleman doing the only thing that is left for him to do, namely to turn to the press to see whether his story can be told?
The Minister of Finance said that parliament must decide, but we must decide in the dark; we must decide blindly; we must decide just on the statement of the minister. We are not allowed even to get the minister before a committee where he can be cross-examined.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; you will have the committee of the whole after second reading.

I believe that in his remarks today the minister gave the whole show away, the whole underlying causes that have culminated in the debate we have before us today, when he told us that the governor of the Bank of Canada had committed the unpardonable sin of issuing an annual report at the normal time, at the same time it is issued every year, but it just happened to be during the election campaign of 1958. These statements always come out in March but because the government for political expediency decided to call an election then the governor of the Bank of Canada, supposed to be free and independent of the cabinet, had the nerve to issue his annual statement at the normal time and it embarrassed the government. I think that was when Mr. Coyne signed his own death warrant.
Then we saw how on May 30 the minister wanted the governor to resign because of some future disagreement they might have. Yet on June 26 he wants him to resign because of past disagreements. It is obvious to me and to many others, Mr. Speaker, that there has been a struggle going on within the government but the struggle has not been between the Minister of Finance and Mr. Coyne because both of them have been on the same side for the last four years. The struggle was between the old Tory orthodox financial policy of Coyne and the Minister of Finance on the one hand and

the political expediency of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on the other. That has been the struggle that has gone on for four years.
You are looking under the bed again.
And the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees).

And the Minister of Trade and Commerce as an hon. member says. Over the last four years the Minister of Finance has always won. He is a pretty tough little scrapper. It is also obvious to everyone that Mr. Coyne is a pretty fair scrapper and when the two of them teamed up apparently they were more than a match for the Prime Minister when he wanted to embark on some of the political expediencies that he thought might be advantageous to the Tory party at the moment.
But this time the other side won. Expediency won, and where did this leave the Minister of Finance? He had to do an about-face. He could not very well do it and save face at the same time, so the only thing he could do was to turn on the man with whom he apparently had no disagreement over a period of four years and make him the goat of the whole thing.
I think that the smallest thing of all has been the way an attempt was made to use the pension of Mr. Coyne as a lever to get him out without his story being told. First of all, I do not want anyone to get the idea that I approve of a $25,000 pension for a man with seven years' service, especially when our old age pensioners are trying to get along on $55 a month. But I want to make one thing very clear. The Tories are responsible for both. The $25,000 pension was approved by the Tory appointees on the board of governors of the Bank of Canada and the $55 pension for old age pensioners is also the responsibility of the present government. So they cannot evade the blame for either one.
It used to be $40.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the Liberals $46. That was their limit.
There we go back into ancient history again.
You started it.

The Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) both made a great to-do about the 10 per cent boost in tariffs advocated by the governor of the Bank of Canada. Our position on tariffs is very well known in the house and I do not think it needs to be reiterated today.
Governor of Bank of Canada
What is it? We don't know.

I should like to know what the difference is between an honest proposal such as put forward by Mr. Coyne and which would be applicable to everyone in the country and the policy of the present government which is to place dictatorial power in the hands of one minister so that nobody will know what is going on and so they can reward their friends and punish their enemies through their tariffs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You do not believe that yourself.

I should like to know what the difference is between an honest proposal such as the governor of the bank made of a 10 per cent increase in tariffs and the method now being adopted by the Minister of Finance. If the Canadian dollar is devaluated, it seems to me that it would have exactly the same effect as if tariffs were increased. People will pay that much more for imports coming into the country. The governor of the bank had an honest way and apparently that is unacceptable to the government.
It is obvious that the governor of the Bank of Canada had to be the sacrificial lamb on the altar of Tory political expediency and that is why he is in the position he is today. We found that the present government was determined to push through the house a bill to make the tariff board a government toy. Now they want the Bank of Canada to be in the same position and because the governor of the bank will not go along with it his head must now come off.
However, Mr. Speaker, there is one thing about which the government is consistent and that is their slogan, do it now. I understand that the term of office of the governor of the Bank of Canada expires around the 1st of December of this year. But the government cannot wait for that. They must do it now and it is obvious why. If they wait for six months their greatest alibi will be gone.
There have been many rumours recently, and I am not sure they are finished, of a federal election in the very near future. That is why we see this attempt to lay the responsibility for all the ills, all the mistakes, all the blunders of four years of Conservative rule on the shoulders of the governor of the Bank of Canada. If the government and its spokesmen, and they have got some "dillies", can pull the wool over the eyes of the Canadian people, if they can make the Canadian people so furious about a $25,000 pension that they will forget that only two years ago the government scrapped an airplane that had
7098	HOUSE OF
Governor of Bank of Canada cost the Canadian taxpayers over $450 million, embarked on another program that cost another $300 million and have now turned around, I understand, and embarked on another program that is going to cost another $300 million to buy a plane inferior to the one they scrapped two years ago, it is no wonder that they want to fight the next election on the issue of a $25,000 pension.
Neither myself nor the other members of my party, Mr. Speaker, have ever agreed with Mr. Coyne or if we have it has been to a very limited extent. We have disagreed with him far more often than we have agreed with him in the past, but we maintain that even our enemies are entitled to a fair trial. If the day ever comes when I find myself saying or doing what the Minister of Finance and the government are asking the house to do today to try, condemn and execute a man without giving him any opportunity for defence, then I will say that I am no longer a democratic member of a democratc country.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
By all means.
From his remarks I take it that he is in favour of increased tariffs. I take it he is in favour of raising present tariffs by 10 per cent? Is that correct?
If the hon. member had attended the house often and had listened attentively, I do not think there would be any question in his mind where I and my party stand on tariffs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You do not want to answer that question.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, my first words are to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for having introduced this bill.
Mr. Coyne, for a long time, has been making fools of our citizens in trying to sabotage the policy of this responsible government of ours.
The speeches he made across the country are a challenge. The annual report of the Bank of Canada was nothing but an election pamphlet. Under this government the governor of the Bank of Canada had become arrogant; he followed in the footsteps of the opposition like economist Lamontagne.
The Minister of Finance, with his usual wisdom and care has always been patient, not wanting to press on unduly, thinking that Coyne, the economist, would come to his senses and would actually discharge his


duties as governor of the Bank of Canada and stop being a political instrument in the hands of the opposition.
In Mr. Coyne's mind the economy of Canada was Mr. Coyne. His attitude is in glaring contradiction with the principles of responsible government. It was time that the Minister of Finance took action because I should not have been surprised if Mr. Coyne had substituted the Queen's picture for his own on our currency.
The people have passed judgment on him. I have visited my riding as all Conservative members do. My constituents told me that it was high time that the government got rid of Mr. Coyne once and for all, and that policy-making be handed back to the responsible government. It would be stupid and illogical to have that man appear before a committee of the house. He is condemned by the public course of action he has chosen. His conduct has been in utter opposition with the minister's.
Logically, he should have resigned without the government having to introduce a bill to that effect. He has instead stood up against a majority decision of the directors of the Bank of Canada. He urged Canadians to save and to tighten their belts while he was having a handsome pension voted for himself.
Here is another argument that condemns him, in my opinion, without any need for a parliamentary committee.
What is serious is that he made public his discussions with the minister. It is unfortunate and hard to understand that Mr. Coyne did not realize the terrible unscrupulousness he was committing.
A minister remains silent at all times about any discussions that take place in a council of ministers.
What is serious, is that out of revenge, Mr. Coyne published a confidential document, namely a memorandum sent by him to the Minister of Finance and containing his views about what should be included in the budget. In so doing the governor threatened the very basis of the whole structure of officialdom and destroyed the secrecy of relations between the cabinet and its advisors.
I must say that I was quite surprised -and interested-to hear the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers) read the section of the act which forbids Mr. Coyne to violate his oath and to divulge secret matters. I think that was sufficient reason for Mr. Coyne to resign without being heard by a committee.
The Minister of Finance was right when he said:

The fact that the governor has chosen to violate the confidential nature of these communications is no reason for the government to do likewise and to make public facts which it has always been agreed are of a confidential character.
The opposition has chosen to ask for a vote to show its disapproval of the minister's conduct. In so doing, however, it went against a tradition which ought to be respected at any cost and which it had itself upheld on January 20, 1960 when the famous confidential report was made public.
I hope that the Senate will act wisely and will not oppose this bill.
Mr. Speaker, it can properly be said that Mr. Coyne has been the executioner of the Canadian economy in collusion with the opposition. I should not be surprised to see him run as a Liberal candidate in Manitoba in the next election.
Mr. Speaker, the point at issue here is whether the representative of the Canadian people is Mr. Coyne or the present government. The case in point is whether we should return to democratic principles and responsible government.
Mr. Speaker, the opposition is in hot water over this bill. They do not know what to do about it. If they confess to the people that they lacked judgment and good sense when they appointed Mr. Coyne as governor a few years ago, they will recognize their lack of responsibility and automatically repudiate the governor's monetary policy. If they vote against this bill, they will give up responsible government for dictatorship.
I will vote for this bill because I am in favour of responsible government.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to one particular aspect of this debate. Many times in the past I have warned the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) about matters in his department having to do with debt, interest rates, fiscal policy and exchange rates. I might say that I have also warned him about matters pertinent to the troubles in which the government now finds itself and particularly the appointment of members of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada, which I feel is pertinent to the troubles which have arisen now between the government and the Bank of Canada.
I have some quotations from statements I placed on Hansard in the past concerning the appointments to the board of directors. In Hansard of March 18, 1959, over two years ago, at page 2037 I had the following to say:
In my opinion there is one fundamental weakness in the Bank of Canada Act. Members of the judiciary are appointed by the different parties when in power and I think they can be said to be above reproach. However, the members of the
Governor of Bank of Canada
board of directors of the Bank of Canada might not always be held to be as much above reproach as they should be. Just the other day, for instance, we heard about one director contributing large sums of money toward the election of different members ...
Conservative members.

That is right.
And then I continued as follows:
I am not accusing any member of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada of not acting in the best interests of Canada but the implication is there that sometimes they may act in a certain way for political reasons. If a man is contributing $20,000 or $25,000 of his own money to a political party, what assurance do we have that the people of Canada will get the best action from him as a director of the Bank of Canada? Will he always have the good of Canada at heart?
Then I went on as follows:
If we look at the list of directors of the Bank of Canada we see that more than one is a recent political appointment.
When I said "more than one" at that time it was rather an understatement. Then I continued as follows:
Our fiscal policy at the present time is not good. We have the highest bank deposits we have ever had in our history. Yet the Minister of Finance cannot get the people to buy his bonds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not true. The last issue was oversubscribed.
The minister was of course right because he used all kinds of tax gimmicks in respect to that particular issue and it was oversubscribed. Then I went on to say this:
He tells us that he requires money. If so, why are there so many bonds held by the banks? I call on the Minister of Finance and the government to have members on the board of directors of the Bank of Canada who have no political axe to grind and who will at all times give their best consideration to the people of Canada and not make decisions based on political reasons.
Then later, on April 14 I again spoke on this subject and called on the government not to make political appointments to the directorship of the Bank of Canada. I went back and read the debate in 1936. I thought I would see what Mr. Dunning, Mr. W. L. Mackenzie King and Mr. Bennett said at that time in connection with the board of directors. On June 1, 1936, as found at page 3257 of Hansard of that date, Hon. Charles A. Dunning, the then minister of finance, moved that the house go into committee to consider a resolution that it was expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Bank of Canada Act in order to provide, among other things, an increase in the capital stock of the bank; to enable the minister of finance to purchase certain shares of the Bank of Canada to assure ownership of a majority of the shares by the government; to increase the number of directors; and to provide for election and appointment of directors in such

Governor of Bank of Canada manner as to assure voting control of the board by directors appointed by the government.
I was struck by this whole debate and by the remarks of those who took part in it. I will quote just one sentence in connection with the election of the various officers of the bank. It is by Hon. Charles A. Dunning, the then minister of finance, and is be found at page 3263 of Hansard of June 1, 1936:
I am sure no member of the committee need have any fear that such appointments will be subject to political pressure or to partisan influences.
It is true that Mr. Dunning that time criticized the election of the first directors under Mr. Bennett, but he criticized them on one point only. He said at that time that the Canadian chamber of commerce, which was an organized business group, had intervened in the election, submitting a slate of nominees all of whom were elected. He also said that he was not criticizing the personnel of the board. In fact, he paid tribute to the various members of that board who had been appointed under Mr. Bennett, and said that they had done a great service for Canada. He was looking to the future. Of course, they were bringing more directors in at that time and he wanted to get away from the position in which one business organization might nominate directors and have elected all the directors whom they nominated. Even Mr. Bennett did not make any political appointments to the board in his time. This resolution resulted in a bill which passed through the house without any division except one, and that was in connection with the chairman's ruling.
In his speech in the house on that day, Mr. Dunning gave some quotations from the speech of the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King when he was leader of the opposition, as found at page 4228 of Hansard of June 22, 1934:
I do think the directorate of the bank ought to be so formed that, whether the pressure is upon the bank from the government on the one side, or upon the government from the financial interests and through the bank on the other, there should be on the board of directors some one or more persons who will be quick to sense the situation, give the danger signal, and arouse the country to the pressure which is being brought to bear. There is the danger of a government bringing too much in the way of pressure to bear on a central bank.
It is interesting to note that in that debate Mr. King, Mr. Dunning, and Mr. Bennett, all three, agreed with that particular argument. This government is carrying on with all political appointments to the board and that is quite contrary to the thinking of our two former prime ministers, namely Mr. King and Mr. Bennett. I heard the hon. member for


Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) say tonight that he represented the constituency that Mr. Bennett represented at one time. He certainly did not put forward any of the arguments put forward by Mr. Bennett in that debate.
Part of the constituency.

If hon. members will read that debate, I do not see how anybody can come to any other conclusion but that our two former prime ministers of this country would consider the present position intolerable in respect of the composition of the board of directors.
My question again to the members of this house is this, and I submitted it two years ago. Would such men, highly political appointees, have the good of Canada at heart or have they the good of the party at heart? Does a director of the Bank of Canada, whose qualification for that position seems to be that he contributed $20,000 to the party funds, have the good of the party at heart or does he have the good of the Canadian people at heart?
According to the reports, the directors of the Bank of Canada one day are on the side of Mr. Coyne; then after they hear from the Minister of Finance, without any change in government policy and without any change in bank policy, they are all against Mr. Coyne, except one. I say that this is irresponsible action on the part of the board of directors. The minister himself admitted that Mr. Coyne did not know what was in the budget. He therefore should not prejudge him. I am sure that Mr. Coyne did not vote- as a matter of fact, he had no vote-for an increase in his pension. If the minister is going to censure anybody in connection with voting that increase in the pension of the governor and the deputy governor, I think he should censure the members of the board of directors appointed by this government. I also think that the minister should have expected some report from the board of directors concerning this action they had taken. I think it is quite consistent with the minister's statements in this house that one or more of the board of directors consulted the minister beforehand and may in fact have received his permission for this increase in pension.
The minister then would be technically right in saying today that he did not know it had been passed if he had not read the minutes of the board of directors and if someone had not told him that the increase was there. He could easily avoid reading these minutes if he thought they contained any material that might be of use to him at some later date, when in trouble, as is the case now. It seems to me that if we as a

parliament discharge a high government officer, responsible only to us in this parliament, without giving him a hearing, even though he may be 100 per cent wrong we are going against all the concepts of justice in the bill of rights.
If the government have a case, as they say they have, I want to vote with the government. I heard one minister say we are contacting Mr. Coyne. I have only seen Mr. Coyne once, and that was at the time he appeared before the committee inquiring into the unemployment insurance fund. As I say, I do not think we can have two sovereignties in one country, but unless we get some information, unless we get the facts I do not see how anybody can vote with any intelligence. It seems to me that the rights of an individual are involved here. The government should not be afraid to have him come before a committee of parliament. They will have a majority there, as they will have a majority in the committee in this house.
If this government does not allow this, I would say that the bill of rights, framed and accompanied by the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) which were meant to immortalize the words of that bill of rights, should be turned face to the wall and never hung face out again unless it is edged in black and draped in mourning, because this is the first great infringement of the bill of rights in the parliament of Canada.

-and frankly what he did was to proceed in a tortuous way to set up men of straw and then try to demolish them. He said the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was pedantic. I would not want to be too unkind to him, but I would say he was almost psychopathic in his personal bitterness toward the Minister of Finance. He lost all reason; he lost all judgment. As a matter of fact, the hon. member is a man who, in attacking the minister and the government for denying, as he says, the rights of parliament,
Governor of Bank of Canada has conveniently forgotten his own actions and attitudes when he was a member of the previous administration.
But you were going to change all this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue

If we were to follow the example of the hon. member from Essex East (Mr. Martin), who delivered what I thought was a rather patronizing lecture to some of the younger members of this house, I might say to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that a man who lives in a glass house should not throw stones.
He is the master of innuendo. That is what we heard this afternoon-innuendo, smear, hypothetical cases concocted in his own mind. He then proceeded to try to place the blame on the minister and the government. He went to ridiculous lengths and thereby showed merely the paucity of his own thinking.
In so far as the hon. member for Essex East is concerned, we heard from him a great lecture on the bill of rights. He talked about the accused having the right to be heard. But, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the question, who is the accused in this case? Is it not the government that is being accused on all sides? Who first laid the charge but the governor? He is the man who ran out into public print and laid the charges of unfair treatment-
He would not be silenced by that arrogant little character over there; that is the reason.
Communist.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
The comments we have just heard of course demonstrate the prejudice that exists in certain minds; the refusal to recognize the situation with a certain amount of objectivity to see what is the principle involved here. The hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) referred to the accused being denied the right to be heard. If-and I say "if" advisedly-the governor is the person who has been accused, then he has certainly been heard. He has had a whole series of advocates, and if we wish to use the simile of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams), in a court of appeal the accused does not appear; he is represented by his advocates. We have Mr. Coyne's advocates all across the other side of the chamber. He is not without voice and he is certainly not on his own.
We have been besieged by an almost schizophrenic frenzy of literature emanating from his headquarters in the Bank of Canada. I will not go into the question of the propriety of the governor using the facilities of the bank in putting forward his own personal

Governor of Bank of Canada case, not the case of the Bank of Canada, and utilizing the facilities of the bank, not only to send some copies of letters to members of parliament but to spread them across the country.
Eight pages today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
The hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate spoke about the fact that two sovereignties could not exist in one country; that they were incompatible. If they admit that, what purpose is being served by their argument? It is wholly sterile. The fact is that the governor has set himself up as a sovereignty and we have the governor of the Bank of Canada challenging the government. That is the clear issue before this house.
Who is responsible for this situation? It is obvious that it is the governor. The governor could have accepted the requested resignation; he could have resigned and governed himself accordingly. He could also have received the request, refused it, kept quiet and carried on his business; or he could have done what he should have done, that is, acceded to the request to resign. If he had a case-
And the Conservative government could start the printing presses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
-to protest, he could have put his case forward. There was no difficulty. We have here a strange precedent that is being sought. The opposition are asking that where a public servant is in disagreement with the government he may demand the right to appear before a committee and that he can cross-examine a minister of the crown before that committee. From that time onward, every public servant would have that right. But, surely, it is completely illogical to consider that a public servant, such as a general in the army who, on disagreeing with a minister would be relieved of his command, could still stay effectively in command bawling his arguments at the top of his voice. That would not be permitted. It would be the same thing in the case of a high public servant, such as a deputy minister, who refused to resign.
The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and others indicated that if there was disagreement between the minister and the governor in 1957 or 1958, this was the occasion to have dealt with the matter. Perhaps he and his friends, too, had prior occasion to disagree with the governor. They did not speak about that. What would have been done at that time, in such a case? What could have been done, except to ask for his resignation? If he had refused, it would only have been possible to have come before this house to
[Mr. Lambert.)

ask for his outright dismissal. The procedure would have been the same and we should have heard the same cries of persecution.
The position of the governor of the Bank of Canada is completely unsupportable. If there is any disagreement with the government he must resign. Opposition speakers did say that the minister was wrong in not disclosing that there had been differences of opinion or disputes earlier but, surely, it is an accepted fact that the first time you have a dispute you do not necessarily rush out to the public and shout from the rooftops that you disagree with this or that person. Certainly, there must be an attempt, and a serious, determined attempt, to overcome those differences and to try to work together. I think there is ample evidence that the minister determined to do just that.
We have heard a great deal about the accused having a chance to speak. But since when is it the accepted practice that the government, if charged, must be wrong unless it proves it is right? That is precisely the burden of the argument put up by the opposition. They are prepared to make all sorts of charges, reasonable or unreasonable, and then the government must prove itself to be right. I put it to hon. gentlemen opposite that he who makes charges must either come forward with the evidence or keep quiet. There is a very trite saying, a very popular saying, that you either put up or shut up. That is what I would say to those who make all these charges, fanciful and otherwise, that the government has misbehaved in this regard. Either they should come forward with facts or else they should keep quiet.
Why has this controversy arisen? It has arisen because the governor of the bank willed it so. He is the man who rushed to the press. As far as the minister is concerned, he did the proper thing in asking the governor for his resignation. The next thing we heard, some 12 days later, was that the governor had issued a statement to the press. Then followed a barrage of correspondence and statements, confidential documents which he spread far and wide; then, again, today, we got this document-a most contemptible document. I say this in all earnestness; it was a most contemptible document deserving nothing but the greatest amount of scorn. Charges of blackmail are made. I am questioning whether the governor of the Bank of Canada is the true author of this document though it is true his signature appears upon it. When we look at it, no man with the degree of responsibility which a governor of the Bank of Canada should possess could stoop to such a document unless he was motivated by reasons other than the proper conduct of his office.

There were on another occasion words used which I think are appropriate to this occasion, and I would apply these words to the governor of the Bank of Canada today. For God's sake, go.
